The folder now holds wheels/, python.tar.gz (or .zip), uv.tar.gz (or .zip), owlet.tar.gz (or .zip), and the docs zip.

items.title: Install on the pit laptop (no internet)
macOS and Linux
items.text:
1. Copy the folder off the stick into your home folder (on Linux the stick is usually under /media/):

    cp -R /Volumes/<stick>/flashpoint-offline ~/

  2. Put uv in ~/.local/bin, and add that folder to your PATH:

    mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
tar -xzf ~/flashpoint-offline/uv.tar.gz -C ~/.local/bin --strip-components=1
~/.local/bin/uv tool update-shell

    Open a new terminal.

  3. Unpack Python where uv looks for it:

    mkdir -p "$(uv python dir)"
tar -xzf ~/flashpoint-offline/python.tar.gz -C "$(uv python dir)"

  4. Install Flashpoint from the folder, with no network:

    uv tool install --offline --no-index --find-links ~/flashpoint-offline/wheels --managed-python --python 3.13 flashpoint

  5. Unpack owlet into Flashpoint's cache:

    mkdir -p ~/.cache/flashpoint
tar -xzf ~/flashpoint-offline/owlet.tar.gz -C ~/.cache/flashpoint

  6. Create your configuration:

    flashpoint init --team <number>

  7. Unzip flashpoint-docs-X.Y.zip into a folder of its own, and open its index.html for these docs. Search may not work from disk; the navigation and links do.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
Run these in PowerShell. E: stands for the stick's drive letter.

  1. Copy the folder off the stick into your home folder:

    Copy-Item -Recurse E:\flashpoint-offline $HOME\

  2. Put uv in .local\bin in your home folder, and add that folder to your PATH:

    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $HOME\.local\bin
Expand-Archive $HOME\flashpoint-offline\uv.zip -DestinationPath $HOME\.local\bin
& "$HOME\.local\bin\uv.exe" tool update-shell

    Open a new PowerShell window.

  3. Unpack Python where uv looks for it:

    $py = uv python dir
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $py
Expand-Archive $HOME\flashpoint-offline\python.zip -DestinationPath $py

  4. Install Flashpoint from the folder, with no network:

    uv tool install --offline --no-index --find-links $HOME\flashpoint-offline\wheels --managed-python --python 3.13 flashpoint

  5. Unpack owlet into Flashpoint's cache:

    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $HOME\.cache\flashpoint
Expand-Archive $HOME\flashpoint-offline\owlet.zip -DestinationPath $HOME\.cache\flashpoint

  6. Create your configuration:

    flashpoint init --team <number>

  7. Unzip flashpoint-docs-X.Y.zip into a folder of its own, and open its index.html for these docs. Search may not work from disk; the navigation and links do.

items.title: If the laptop already has Python 3.11 to 3.14: pip instead of uv
items.text:
You can skip uv and the Python download, and install the wheels into a virtual environment with pip. Download the wheels in step 2 with that Python's version in --python-version, such as 3.12. Then, on macOS and Linux:

python3.13 -m venv ~/flashpoint-venv
~/flashpoint-venv/bin/python -m pip install --no-index --find-links ~/flashpoint-offline/wheels flashpoint

On Windows:

py -3.13 -m venv $HOME\flashpoint-venv
& $HOME\flashpoint-venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --no-index --find-links $HOME\flashpoint-offline\wheels flashpoint

The command is then ~/flashpoint-venv/bin/flashpoint ($HOME\flashpoint-venv\Scripts\flashpoint.exe on Windows), or plain flashpoint after you activate the environment. Unpack owlet as in step 5.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
$ flashpoint --version
flashpoint 0.2.0

Then run flashpoint doctor. Its python line shows the Python 3.13 you brought, its owlet cache line shows the folder you unpacked into, and the owlet check says downloaded, verified. On a Mac it looks like this; Linux and Windows show linuxx86-64 or windowsx86-64 and their own home folder:

python     3.13.<n> on macosuniversal
...
owlet cache /Users/<you>/.cache/flashpoint/owlet
...
  ok       owlet for hoot format C19    owlet 26.3.0 downloaded, verified

Before the first import, doctor checks only the newest hoot format Flashpoint knows. After you import hoots, it checks each format in the lake, so an older season's owlet shows up then.

Last, import one hoot with networking still off:

flashpoint ingest <a .hoot file>

It ends with 1 ingested and no FAILED line. If it says failed (owlet-download-failed), will retry, the owlet for that hoot's format isn't in the cache: see owlet isn't downloaded, or its checksum doesn't match. If flashpoint isn't found, see flashpoint isn't found after installing.

items.title: Live CAN health
items.text:
Status: experimental. Live CAN needs robot code that publishes CAN health (below), and it can report false dropouts on fast buses: on our robot's CANivore, with signals at 250 Hz, gaps under 15 ms were counted as dropouts. Until a per-bus dropout window (#66) lands and the pit check on a real robot passes, treat a lone dropout on a fast bus with suspicion and confirm it in Replay's CAN health.

The Live CAN view shows, while you work on the robot, which CTRE device dropped out, rebooted or faulted, and whether it was one device or the whole bus. Use it to find loose CAN and power connectors:

  • Shake test (robot disabled): wiggle each harness, one at a time, and watch for a dropout on the device you're touching.
  • Drive test (robot enabled): drive hard, and see which devices drop or reboot under load.

The same view serves both: every event is tagged ENABLED or DISABLED, so there's no mode to switch. A 40 ms dropout is invisible to the eye and to a 2 Hz dashboard, but it shows here, because robot code counts dropouts every loop and the view only shows what the count did.

Live CAN reads the robot, not the lake. It records nothing: when you're done, nothing has changed in the lake or the configuration. For the exact picture after a match (frame by frame, from the hoot logs), use CAN health in Replay and History.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• flashpoint serve works on a laptop that can reach the robot: on its Wi-Fi, by USB, or tethered.
  • Flashpoint knows the robot's address: a team number (flashpoint init --team <number>) or hosts in acquire.toml. Live CAN uses the same addresses as flashpoint acquire. For another address, start serve with --robot-host.
  • A robot file whose project is the project name robot code publishes. Without one, every device shows UNMAPPED.
  • Robot code publishes CAN health. Until it does, the view says the robot "is not publishing live CAN health". The next section adds it.

items.title: Adding it to robot code
items.text:
CanHealthPublisher.java is a suggestion, not a library: copy it into your robot project and adapt it. It's tested with WPILib 2026.2.1 and Phoenix 6 26.3.0 (the line at the top of the file), so check it against your versions. The sample project's Robot.java wires it up next to the other samples.

  1. Copy CanHealthPublisher.java into your robot project.
  2. Create one publisher with your project's name. Use the name your wpilog metadata uses (build info), so the view finds your robot file.
  3. In robotInit(), add every TalonFX, CANcoder and Pigeon 2 with the signal to watch, then addBus each bus.
  4. Call periodic() from robotPeriodic().
  5. Deploy, and check the loop time (below).
private final CanHealthPublisher canHealth = new CanHealthPublisher("Robot-2026");

public void robotInit() {
  canHealth.add("DriveTrain", frontLeftDrive, frontLeftDrive.getPosition());
  canHealth.add("DriveTrain", frontLeftEncoder, frontLeftEncoder.getPosition());
  canHealth.add("DriveTrain", pigeon, pigeon.getYaw());
  canHealth.add("rio", intakeRoller, intakeRoller.getVelocity());
  // ... every TalonFX, CANcoder and Pigeon 2
  canHealth.addBus("rio");
  canHealth.addBus("DriveTrain");
}

public void robotPeriodic() {
  canHealth.periodic();
}
  • For each device, pass the signal to watch. Pick one updated at 50 Hz or faster (position or velocity on a motor, position on a CANcoder, yaw on a Pigeon 2): a dropout counts when that signal is older than 2.5 of its own update periods, so a slow signal only catches long dropouts.
  • The sample has add for TalonFX, CANcoder and Pigeon 2 only. For another CTRE device (a CANdle, CANrange or TalonFXS), add an add overload in your copy, or its slot in your robot file shows MISSING.
  • periodic() refreshes every watched signal once per loop with one BaseStatusSignal.refreshAll call per bus, keeps the totals, and publishes every 5 loops (100 ms, NetworkTables' own rate). Bus status is read every half second.

Check the loop time before a competition. The sample should cost well under 1 ms per loop for 30 devices, but measure it: watch the loop-time overrun warnings in the Driver Station, or log Timer.getFPGATimestamp() around canHealth.periodic(). If it costs too much, watch fewer signals or publish less often.

items.title: Run a shake or drive test
items.text:
1. Turn the robot on, with robot code running, and join the laptop to its network.

  2. Start the app:

    flashpoint serve

    To use another robot address:

    flashpoint serve --robot-host <robot address>

  3. Open the LIVE CAN tab. It connects to the robot while the view is open. Wait for the pill to read CONNECTED.

  4. Type what you're about to do in MARK ("now wiggling: FL module") and press Enter or SET. Every event after that carries the mark until you change it or press CLEAR.
  5. For a shake test, keep the robot disabled and wiggle one harness at a time, changing the mark as you go. For a drive test, enable and drive hard.
  6. Watch the device cards and the EVENTS log. A device that dropped shows DROPPED for 5 seconds, and the log gets a DROPOUT line with the mark.
  7. Confirm what you found after the match in Replay's CAN health, from the hoot logs.

Marks and the event log stay in your browser only: reloading the page clears them, and other people watching don't see them. Device totals come from the server: everyone watching sees the same totals, and they survive a reload. They start again from zero when nobody has had the view open for about 30 seconds.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
• The pill reads CONNECTED, and the robot line shows the robot's address, "project" and the robot code's project name, and "config" and the robot file it matched.
  • Each bus has a panel with its UTILISATION and error counts, then a card per device, by slot. A device that's heard and has nothing new reads OK.
  • Before anything happens, EVENTS says "No events yet. They appear here as the robot reports them." Once the robot reports one, each dropout, reboot or fault is a line there, with the time, ENABLED or DISABLED, and your mark.
  • No robot to hand? The fake robot (below) makes a device drop out every few seconds, so you can see what a dropout looks like.

Every state, pill and event is described in the Live CAN view reference.

items.title: Isolated or bus-wide
items.text:
When several devices on one bus drop out in the same update, the cause is usually the bus (a CAN wire, the CANivore's USB, a terminator), not each device. Flashpoint applies the same rule as CAN health: a dropout is bus-wide when at least half of the bus's other reporting devices also dropped in that update. It's shown as one bus event and isn't counted against any device. Otherwise it's isolated, charged to that device.

Updates arrive about every 100 ms, so a dropout that crosses two updates can show as two isolated dropouts instead of one bus-wide one. CAN health's after-match view has the exact timing.

items.title: When robot code restarts
items.text: Totals count from when robot code started. When they go down, Flashpoint takes it as a robot code restart: it logs one RESTART event and starts counting again, without reporting the drop as dropouts or reboots.

items.title: Without a robot: the fake robot
items.text:
Flashpoint has a fake robot that publishes the contract for Ignite's 2026 robot, for trying the view or working on it. Run it from a Flashpoint checkout (developer guide); a uv or pipx install can't run it with plain python:

poetry run python -m flashpoint.live.fake_robot --scenario shake
flashpoint serve --robot-host 127.0.0.1

Scenarios: shake (disabled, one device at a time drops out), drive (enabled, bus-wide drops, reboots and bus errors), restart (totals climb, then robot code restarts). --period sets the seconds between updates. Stop it with Ctrl-C.

items.title: The contract
items.text:
Robot code publishes these NetworkTables topics, all under /Flashpoint/Live/CANHealth/. <bus> is the bus name your robot code uses (rio, or a CANivore's name such as DriveTrain); <Model>-<id> is the hoot device name (such as TalonFX-11), so it reads the same as Replay and your robot file. Totals count from when robot code started; "since the last update" values cover the time since robot code last published.

Topic Type Meaning Version integer Contract version: 1 Project string The robot code's project name, as in the wpilog metadata (such as Robot-2026). Picks the robot file: the one with this project, latest season first Enabled boolean Whether the robot is enabled <bus>/<Model>-<id>/Connected boolean Whether the device is heard right now <bus>/<Model>-<id>/Dropouts integer Robot loops (a running total) in which the device's watched status signal was older than 2.5 times its update period <bus>/<Model>-<id>/MaxAgeMs double The oldest that signal was in any loop since the last update, in milliseconds <bus>/<Model>-<id>/Resets integer Device resets robot code has seen (a running total) <bus>/<Model>-<id>/Faults integer Faults seen at any point since the last update, as bits: 0 under-voltage, 1 boot during enable, 2 hardware, 3 bridge brownout, 4 bad magnet <bus>/<Model>-<id>/MinSupplyV double The lowest supply voltage since the last update <bus>/Bus/Utilization double Fraction of the bus in use, 0 to 1 <bus>/Bus/BusOffCount integer Times the bus went off (a running count) <bus>/Bus/TxFullCount integer Times the transmit buffer was full (a running count) <bus>/Bus/ReceiveErrorCount integer Receive error counter <bus>/Bus/TransmitErrorCount integer Transmit error counter

A topic with the wrong type, or a negative count, is ignored and noted on its device. The rest keeps working. If Version isn't 1, the view shows nothing but a message naming both versions: update Flashpoint or the robot code so they match.

Keep these topics where they are. Don't move them under /Flashpoint/CANBus/ to sit next to the bus-status logger. When robot code logs NetworkTables to its wpilog, these topics are written as NT:/Flashpoint/Live/..., which Flashpoint's flashpoint season root (/Flashpoint/) doesn't match, so they never mix with the DataLog entries under /Flashpoint/CANBus/ that CAN health reads.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
The view says Check CONNECTING or NOT CONNECTED, and stays there The laptop can reach the robot (ping 10.TE.AM.2), robot code is running, and the address is right (--robot-host) No robot address Run flashpoint init --team <number>, or start with --robot-host. If you already set a team, acquire.toml may not load: run flashpoint doctor to see why NOT PUBLISHING Robot code doesn't publish under /Flashpoint/Live/CANHealth/: add the publisher, or check it runs UNSUPPORTED VERSION Flashpoint and the robot code use different contract versions Every device UNMAPPED, and "no robot configuration has project …" project in your robot file must equal the published Project A device UNMAPPED Its bus name isn't in the robot file's BUSES table, or its model or CAN id differ from the slot's

For setup problems the view doesn't name, such as no team number, see Troubleshooting: No team number, or run flashpoint doctor.

items.title: Move Flashpoint to another laptop
items.text: Move the lake and your configuration to a new laptop without losing any history or triage. The usual way is to restore the new laptop from your backup. If you have no backup, copy the two folders instead.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• A new laptop that Flashpoint runs on: macOS 13 or later, Linux with glibc 2.35 or later, or Windows on an x86-64 PC (Install).
  • Internet on the new laptop: for the install, for the backup, and to download owlet again for the hoots.
  • Either a backup that's up to date (Back up the lake), or the old laptop at hand to copy from.
  • Time: the rebuild after a restore converts every hoot again.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. On the old laptop, stop anything that writes to the lake: the acquire watch or its service, and flashpoint serve. On Linux, systemctl --user stop flashpoint-acquire; on Windows, schtasks /End /TN flashpoint-acquire.

  2. On the old laptop, make sure the backup has everything. Run flashpoint backup, then flashpoint doctor: the Backup check should be ok, with nothing waiting:

      ok       Backup                       last backup 0 min ago

  3. On the new laptop, install uv and Flashpoint, following the Install page for that computer:

    uv tool install --python 3.13 flashpoint

    Don't run flashpoint init yet. restore brings your configuration back only into an empty config folder.

  4. Install rclone on the new laptop (rclone's install page) and make the same remote with rclone config. Give it the same name as on the old laptop, such as gdrive.

  5. Restore into a new lake:

    macOS and LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    flashpoint restore --remote gdrive:flashpoint --lake ~/flashpoint-lake

    flashpoint restore --remote gdrive:flashpoint --lake "$HOME\flashpoint-lake"

    It prints how many files it restored, and restored the configuration into <config folder>.

  6. Re-point the lake. The restored acquire.toml, in the config folder (~/.config/flashpoint/ on macOS and Linux, %APPDATA%\flashpoint on Windows), still names the old laptop's lake folder in lake. Change it to the new one:

    lake = "/Users/pit/flashpoint-lake"

    On Windows, write the path in single quotes so the backslashes stay as they are: lake = 'C:\Users\Pit\flashpoint-lake'.

  7. Rebuild everything from the raw logs. This downloads owlet the first time it meets a hoot:

    flashpoint rebuild

  8. If the old laptop ran automatic import, set it up here (Run it in the background), and remove it from the old laptop. Two laptops backing up to the same remote replace each other's copy of the lake's metadata.

items.title: Or copy the folders
items.text:
With no backup, copy the folders by hand, after step 1:

  1. Copy the whole lake folder (~/flashpoint-lake by default) and the whole config folder from the old laptop to the new one, on a USB drive or over the network.
  2. Install Flashpoint on the new laptop (step 3 above), without running flashpoint init.
  3. Put the config folder where Flashpoint looks: ~/.config/flashpoint/ on macOS and Linux, %APPDATA%\flashpoint on Windows.
  4. Re-point lake in acquire.toml to where you put the lake (step 6 above).
  5. Run flashpoint doctor. If its lake section says some files are from an older pipeline version (the new laptop has a newer Flashpoint), run flashpoint rebuild.

The owlet cache (~/.cache/flashpoint/) doesn't need copying; Flashpoint downloads it again.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
Run flashpoint doctor on the new laptop:

  • lake names the new folder, and counts the files at each stage, the same number as on the old laptop.
  • config names the config folder, and the robot check names your robot.
  • The owlet check for each hoot format says owlet <version> downloaded, verified.
  • After a restore, the Backup check is ok: the restore counts as a backup, since everything restored is on the remote.

Then run flashpoint serve: Replay lists the same matches, and Anomalies keeps your triage.

If Replay is empty, the app is probably reading a different lake: see Replay says "No Replay data". For Windows paths, see Windows paths and quoting.

items.title: Open a match in AdvantageScope
items.text:
Replay's OPEN IN ADVANTAGESCOPE opens a match's wpilog in AdvantageScope, for a frame-by-frame look at everything robot code logged. Flashpoint finds the match's logs in the lake, puts them in a folder under readable names, and starts AdvantageScope on the wpilog. You add the hoots from that folder yourself.

It works only on the laptop running flashpoint serve, with the app opened on that laptop.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• AdvantageScope is installed on the laptop that runs serve. The WPILib installer includes it. Flashpoint looks for it in this order:
    1. the path under [advantagescope] in report.toml, when it's set;
    2. the newest WPILib year: ~/wpilib/<year>/advantagescope/ on macOS and Linux, C:\Users\Public\wpilib\<year>\advantagescope\ on Windows;
    3. a standalone install: /Applications/AdvantageScope.app on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\AdvantageScope\AdvantageScope.exe on Windows, or advantagescope on the PATH on Linux.
  • serve runs the usual way, without --host 0.0.0.0. Shared on the network, nothing can be launched, not even on the laptop itself.
  • The match has a wpilog. A match with hoots only has nothing to open: download its hoots instead.

items.title: Open the match
items.text:
1. Check that Flashpoint finds AdvantageScope:

    flashpoint doctor

    The AdvantageScope: line names the program and how it was found, such as (WPILib 2026). If it says AdvantageScope: not found, go to Set the path first.

  2. Start the app and open it on this laptop, at http://127.0.0.1:8000/:

    flashpoint serve

  3. In REPLAY, pick the match.

  4. In the DETAILS rail on the right, press OPEN IN ADVANTAGESCOPE. AdvantageScope opens with the match's wpilog. On macOS, if it's already running, it opens a new window.
  5. To add the hoots, use File › Insert log in AdvantageScope and pick them from the folder the panel shows.

The folder is under your computer's temporary folder, in flashpoint-as/<match key>/. Each file is named <match key>__<wpilog or bus>__<original name>. The lake's own copies are never changed. serve removes folders older than a day when it starts.

items.title: Set the path
items.text:
If AdvantageScope is somewhere Flashpoint doesn't look, tell it where:

  1. In the app, open SETUP, then CHECKS. The AdvantageScope line says "not found: install WPILib, or set its path, to open logs from Replay".
  2. Press Set AdvantageScope path, and enter the full path to the program, such as /Applications/AdvantageScope.app on macOS or C:\Users\Public\wpilib\2026\advantagescope\AdvantageScope (WPILib).exe on Windows. Flashpoint checks the path exists, then writes it to report.toml.
  3. Stop serve (Ctrl-C) and start it again. serve looks for AdvantageScope when it starts, so the Replay button uses the new path only after a restart.

Or edit report.toml in your config folder yourself. On Windows, use single quotes so the backslashes stay as they are:

[advantagescope]
path = 'C:\Users\Public\wpilib\2026\advantagescope\AdvantageScope (WPILib).exe'

Clear path to go back to the WPILib or standalone install.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
After step 4 the panel says:

Opened <match key>__wpilog__<file>.wpilog in AdvantageScope.
To add the hoots, use File › Insert log in AdvantageScope and pick them from:
<folder>

followed by the hoot files. A hoot whose end is missing (the robot lost power while writing it) is marked INCOMPLETE. AdvantageScope shows the wpilog's fields in its sidebar.

If the panel says "AdvantageScope did not open:" and a reason, or shows "Open in AdvantageScope is only available on the machine running Flashpoint" in place of the button, the reason says what to fix: open the app on the laptop running serve, at 127.0.0.1, and start serve without --host. If doctor says configured AdvantageScope path not found: <path>, see AdvantageScope path not found.

A static export on a USB stick has no button, only the downloads (Take Replay on a USB stick).

items.title: Take Replay on a USB stick
items.text:
flashpoint report --static writes Replay into a folder that opens from index.html, on any computer, with no install and no network. Use it to hand matches to a drive coach, a mentor at home, or a team without Flashpoint.

Only Replay is in the export. History, Anomalies, Setup and Live CAN need flashpoint serve.
path: Take Replay on a USB stick

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• The lake has at least one imported match. With no logs imported, report stops with no derived sessions in <lake>; run `flashpoint ingest` first.
  • A USB stick with room for it. Replay data is about 1 MB per match, and the raw logs are added on top: the wpilog and every hoot of each match. For a small stick, leave the raw logs out with --no-raw.
  • Set the team name and colours first if you want them on the stick (Set the team name and colours). The export uses them as they are when you write it.
path: Take Replay on a USB stick

items.title: Write the export
items.text:
1. Plug in the stick. Pick a folder on it that is new or empty, such as flashpoint. Flashpoint refuses a folder that has other files in it, unless it's an earlier export, which it replaces.

  2. Run report with --static and that folder.

    macOS:

    flashpoint report --static /Volumes/<stick>/flashpoint

    Linux (the stick is usually under /media/ and your user name):

    flashpoint report --static /media/<you>/<stick>/flashpoint

    Windows (use the stick's drive letter):

    flashpoint report --static E:\flashpoint

    To leave the raw logs out, add --no-raw:

    flashpoint report --static /Volumes/<stick>/flashpoint --no-raw

  3. Wait for the exported line (below), then eject the stick the usual way before you unplug it.

  4. On the other computer, open the stick's flashpoint folder and double-click index.html. It opens in the default browser.

report first builds Replay data for any match that needs it, then exports. The export holds every match that has Replay data, not only new ones; --match and --event limit the build, not the export. To update the stick after new matches or a change of colours, run the same command again. It replaces the folder's contents.
path: Take Replay on a USB stick

items.title: What works on the stick
items.text:
Works Doesn't The match list, filters, tracks, markers, zoom, the readout and COMPARE Zooming past the stored resolution: the window line reads "bucket resolution (n ms)" Downloading each match's wpilog and hoots, unless you used --no-raw OPEN IN ADVANTAGESCOPE: there's no button, only the downloads Anomaly badges on the tracks, as they were when you exported. Each says when its snapshot was taken Opening an anomaly: the Anomalies view isn't in the export Your team name and colours, as they were when you exported History, Anomalies, Setup and Live CAN

With --no-raw, the downloads are replaced by "Raw logs not included in this export. Their lake hashes:" and a hash per log.

The export holds no folder path from the laptop that made it, so it is safe to hand out.
path: Take Replay on a USB stick

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
report ends with two lines like these:

built 2, unchanged 10, removed 0; 12 match(es) listed in 3.1s
exported 12 match(es) to /Volumes/<stick>/flashpoint (36 raw file(s)); open /Volumes/<stick>/flashpoint/index.html

With --no-raw the second line says (0 raw file(s), not included). If it says export failed: <folder> is not empty and is not a previous Flashpoint export, pick a new folder on the stick.

Open index.html. The header shows a STATIC EXPORT pill on the right, and REPLAY is the only tab. Pick a match: its tracks and markers show, as they do in serve.

If Replay says No Replay data, or a match says "This export does not include it.", see Replay says "No Replay data". The Replay view reference describes every part of the screen.
path: Take Replay on a USB stick

items.title: Set up a robot file
items.text: A robot file tells Flashpoint which motor is which. You rarely write one from scratch: Flashpoint drafts it from a log, and you name the motors. This page is the order to do it in. Every key is in the robot file reference.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• Flashpoint installed, and a configuration made with flashpoint init (Install). Without a configuration, nothing is drafted.
  • One match's logs from the robot: the .wpilog and its .hoot files (Import logs from a USB stick). The draft on import needs both. Draft robot in the Setup view needs only the hoots.
  • Internet the first time you import a hoot, so Flashpoint can download owlet, CTRE's hoot converter.
  • Someone who knows the robot: which CAN id is which motor.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Import a match from the robot:

    flashpoint ingest <folder>

    If the log's season has no robot file yet, the import drafts one from the match with the most CAN devices, and says so:

    drafted robot 2026-comp from 2026gacmp_qm7 (22 devices) into /home/pit/.config/flashpoint/robots/2026-comp.toml: name each slot's subsystem and role in Setup > Robots

    It drafts one file per robot-code project: <season>-comp, then <season>-practice for a second project. If you see this line, go to step 3.

  2. If nothing was drafted, use Draft robot. That happens with hoot-only logs, with flashpoint ingest --no-robot-draft, and for a second robot in a season that already has a robot file: a season with any robot file is never drafted into.

    1. Run flashpoint serve and open http://127.0.0.1:8000/#view=setup&tab=draft.
    2. Pick an imported log in the list, then press DRAFT FROM THIS LOG. Every CAN device in its hoots becomes a slot.
    3. Check ROBOT ID. It's also the file's name, such as 2026-practice.
    4. Press SAVE ROBOT. The lake rebuilds in the background: "Saved file. Rebuilding the lake in the background; reload Replay when it finishes (a minute or two)."

    The Setup view reference explains each line of the draft.

  3. Name the slots. In Setup, open CONFIGURATION and find your robot under ROBOTS. Each drafted slot has an id made of its model and CAN id, such as talonfx-11, and an empty SUBSYSTEM and ROLE. Fill them in: subsystem drivetrain, role front-left drive. Keep the drafted slot ids. Press SAVE.

    You can name them later. Until you do, History and anomalies name those slots by CAN id. To edit the file in a text editor instead, it's in the robots/ folder of your config folder (~/.config/flashpoint/robots/ on macOS and Linux, %APPDATA%\flashpoint\robots\ on Windows).

  4. Tie the robot code's bus names to the hoot's buses, if the robot code logs CAN bus status. The draft fills these in for the rio and a single CANivore. With more than one CANivore, add a row for each in the BUSES table, or a [[bus]] table in the file ([[bus]]).

  5. Add signals, if you want a NetworkTables or wpilog value in Flashpoint, such as a subsystem's state. Use the SIGNALS table in Setup, or [[signal]] tables in the file ([[signal]]). A signal's root must be defined in the season file; the bundled one leaves the robot root commented out until you set it.

  6. Group motors that do the same job, so the SIBLING anomaly method can compare them. Setup has no table for this, so edit the file:

    [[siblings]]
name = "drive"
slots = ["talonfx-11", "talonfx-12", "talonfx-13", "talonfx-14"]

    See [[siblings]].

  7. Pick a battery proxy: a low-current device on the main power bus, such as the gyro. Replay's battery track and the brownout markers use its supply voltage. Add the key near the top of the file, above the first [[slot]], so TOML reads it as a top-level key:

    battery_proxy = "pigeon2-1"

    Don't pick a motor (The battery proxy).

  8. After any edit to the file, or a SAVE in Setup, rebuild every session with the new mapping:

    flashpoint derive --all

    You don't need to import the logs again.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
Run flashpoint doctor. The robots section lists the file, its season, its project and its counts:

robots     /home/pit/.config/flashpoint/robots
  2026-comp      season 2026 project Robot-2026: 22 slots, 0 signals

The robot check names it:

  ok       Robot for 2026               2026-comp

While a drafted file still has slots with no subsystem, it's a warning instead, and says how many:

  WARN     Robot for 2026               2026-comp: 4 of 22 slots unnamed (drafted automatically): History and anomalies name them by CAN id
                                        fix: name each slot's subsystem and role in Setup > Robots

In Replay, the match no longer shows robot "unknown".

If the file doesn't load, doctor names the file and the key: see A settings file doesn't load and the robot file's common errors. If matches still show robot "unknown", see The robot shows as "unknown".

items.title: Share logs privately for a bug report
items.text:
Logs from other teams' robots are the most useful thing you can give us: every team logs a little differently, and Flashpoint only gets better at reading them by seeing them. This page says which files to send and how to send them so they stay private.

Never attach .wpilog or .hoot files to a public issue or discussion. They hold your team's match data: every NetworkTables value robot code logs, Driver Station inputs, match data, and every CTRE device's serial number (what a log contains). Treat logs like your robot code.
path: Share logs privately for a bug report

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• You know which match or log shows the problem.
  • You can share a folder from Google Drive, Dropbox or a similar service with one person.
  • Ask your mentor before you send team logs outside the team.
path: Share logs privately for a bug report

items.title: Send the logs
items.text:
1. Open a bug report with the bug form. Fill it in as usual, including flashpoint --version and the flashpoint doctor output. Name the log files and say what's in them, but don't attach them. Say that you have logs to share.
  2. Wait for a maintainer to reply on the issue with how to send them, usually a Google Drive or Dropbox link shared only with them.
  3. Collect the files for the match, the wpilog and every hoot from the same time:
    • From Flashpoint: in REPLAY, pick the match. Under OPEN IN ADVANTAGESCOPE in the DETAILS rail there is a download link for each raw log: ⇩ wpilog, and ⇩ hoot · with the bus. Download each one. They're saved as <match key>__<wpilog or bus>__<original name>. HISTORY has the same links under LOGS for each of a unit's recent matches.
    • From where you copied them: the original files from the robot or the USB stick work just as well. Use these for a practice or pit log, which Replay doesn't list, and for a file that failed to import or was quarantined.
  4. Put the files in one folder and upload it through the private route the maintainer gave you. Share it with that person only, not with "anyone with the link".
  5. Reply on the issue that the logs are shared. Don't post the link or the files there.

Logs shared with us are used only to test Flashpoint, and are deleted when you ask. We don't publish them or pass them on.
path: Share logs privately for a bug report

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
• The issue page has no .wpilog, .hoot or .zip attachments, and no link to the shared folder.
  • The shared folder lists the wpilog and each hoot of the match, with the match key at the start of each name if you downloaded them from Replay.
  • The maintainer confirms on the issue that they have them.

If a file wouldn't import, include its ingest line in the issue, such as QUARANTINED <file>: <reason>. A file was quarantined explains the reasons. The Privacy and network page lists everything a log and the lake hold.
path: Share logs privately for a bug report

items.title: Show the app on the pit network
items.text:
flashpoint serve --host 0.0.0.0 lets other devices on the same network, such as a mentor's laptop or a drive coach's tablet, open the app from the pit laptop. They see the same lake, read-only.

There's no password: anyone on that network who knows the laptop's address can see everything in the lake. The app is read-only then (for everyone, including the laptop itself), so nobody can change triage or settings, but they can read and download your logs. Only do it on a network you trust, and stop it (Ctrl-C) when you're done. Privacy and network lists what a lake holds.
path: Show the app on the pit network

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• flashpoint serve works on the laptop on its own (User guide: Look at the data).
  • The laptop and the other devices are on the same network, and it's one you trust.
  • Do any triage, Setup changes or AdvantageScope launches first, or after you stop sharing. None of them work while the app is shared.
path: Show the app on the pit network

items.title: Share it
items.text:
1. Stop any flashpoint serve already running (Ctrl-C in its terminal).

  2. Start it shared:

    flashpoint serve --host 0.0.0.0

    If the laptop's firewall asks whether to allow incoming connections, allow them, or the other devices can't reach it.

  3. Find the laptop's IP address on that network.

    macOS (en0 is usually Wi-Fi; if it prints nothing, try en1):

    ipconfig getifaddr en0

    Linux (the first address is usually the one):

    hostname -I

    Windows: run ipconfig and use the IPv4 Address under the adapter that's on the pit network.

    ipconfig

  4. On the other device, open http://<laptop IP>:8000/ in a browser, for example http://192.168.1.20:8000/.

  5. When you're done, press Ctrl-C in the terminal. To make changes again, start flashpoint serve without --host.

To use another port, add --port, such as flashpoint serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080, and put that port in the address instead of 8000.
path: Show the app on the pit network

items.title: What others can and can't do
items.text:
Works for everyone Doesn't work, for anyone, the laptop included Replay, History, Anomalies and Setup, to look at Triage: "Read-only: triage is only available on the machine running Flashpoint." Downloading raw logs from Replay Setup fixes and saves, and Appearance changes Live CAN, which changes nothing. The laptop holds the one connection to the robot OPEN IN ADVANTAGESCOPE: "Open in AdvantageScope is only available on the machine running Flashpoint. Use the downloads below."

Sensitivity and grouping in Anomalies, and marks in Live CAN, are each viewer's own. In Replay, COPY LINK can't reach the clipboard on a plain http:// address from another device: it still reads COPIED, so copy the address bar instead.
path: Show the app on the pit network

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
When it starts, serve prints a warning and then the address it serves on:

WARNING: serving on 0.0.0.0 shares the lake's data and raw logs with everyone on the pit network, read-only and with no password.
Flashpoint (lake <lake>) at http://127.0.0.1:8000/

The banner shows 127.0.0.1, the laptop's own address. Other devices use the laptop's IP from step 3.

On the other device, the app opens on Replay with your matches. Open SETUP: under the band it says "Read-only: this app is shared on the network (or not opened on the computer running it). Run the commands shown on that computer."

If serve says cannot listen on 0.0.0.0:8000: and a reason, another program has the port: use --port. For anything else, start at Troubleshooting.
path: Show the app on the pit network

items.title: Start a new season
items.text: Flashpoint doesn't need to be reinstalled each year, but a new season needs a few things before its first event: a Flashpoint that reads the new hoots, a season file, and a robot file for the new robot. Last season's logs, robot file and motor history stay as they are.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• Kickoff has happened, and the new robot code runs and writes logs (a .wpilog and its hoots).
  • Internet, for the update and for the first hoot of the season (owlet).
  • For 2027: Flashpoint 0.3.1 or later. See The 2027 season below.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
Do these after kickoff, when the new robot code first runs.

  1. Update Flashpoint. A new season's CTRE hoot format needs a Flashpoint that knows its owlet.

    uv tool upgrade flashpoint

    If you installed with pipx, run pipx upgrade flashpoint instead. Your config folder and lake are kept (Update Flashpoint). An older Flashpoint quarantines the new hoots with unsupported-compliancy:<n>, and doctor says:

      PROBLEM  owlet for hoot format C<n>   the lake has C<n> hoots, which this Flashpoint can't read

    If that happened, update, then retry those files from the lake's own copies:

    flashpoint rebuild --quarantined

  2. Check the season file. Flashpoint ships a season file for each year it knows: this version ships 2025, 2026 and 2027. flashpoint init copies only the current season and earlier ones into your config folder, so a later year (2027, for a configuration made in 2026) is read from Flashpoint itself, and a fix to it in a Flashpoint update reaches you.

    • To change a root (for example to add your robot code's robot root), copy that year's file into seasons/ in your config folder. Your copy then wins, and later fixes to the bundled file no longer reach it.
    • For a year Flashpoint doesn't ship yet, copy seasons/<last year>.toml to seasons/<this year>.toml and change season =.
    • Without a season file, a robot file that declares signals doesn't load; doctor names the file to create.

    The season file reference has every key.

  3. Add the robot file. Ingest a log from the new robot, with internet so owlet downloads:

    flashpoint ingest <folder>

    The new season has no robot file yet, so the import drafts one, robots/<year>-comp.toml (then <year>-practice for a second robot-code project), with this season's year and project name. Name its slots in Setup > Robots, or use Draft robot in the Setup view for hoot-only logs (Set up a robot file). Last season's robot file stays, so its logs keep their mapping.

    A log's season is the calendar year it was recorded in. Logs from December testing of next season's robot count as this season, so give that robot a file for this season too, or wait until January (Which robot file a log uses).

  4. Check the robot code still writes the CAN inventory, bus status and build info entries. A new robot project is easy to start without them.

  5. Keep the motor list. The motor list (units/units-seed.csv) carries over. Add the new season's motors, and don't remove or relabel old ones: a motor reused on the new robot keeps its history by serial number (Units).

  6. Run flashpoint doctor. From January 1 it checks for a robot for the new year. Until the lake has logs from the new year, that check is a warning that says so, not a problem:

      WARN     Robot for 2027               no robot configured for season 2027; the lake has no 2027 logs yet (the first import of this season's logs drafts one)

    Once the lake has logs from the new year, it's a problem until a robot is configured.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
After your first import of the new season, flashpoint doctor shows:

  • the robot check ok, naming the new robot, or a warning about unnamed slots if you haven't named them yet:

      ok       Robot for 2027               2027-comp

  • an owlet check for the format your new hoots use, downloaded:

      ok       owlet for hoot format C<n>   owlet <version> downloaded, verified

  • the new robot under robots, with season 2027 and the new project name.

The new season's matches are in Replay, and History still has last season's motors.

If the owlet check is a problem, see Hoots this version can't read. If the robot check is a problem, see No robot for this season.

items.title: The 2027 season
items.text:
This version of Flashpoint is ready for January 1, 2027, but not for 2027 hoots:

  • 2027 hoots need Flashpoint 0.3.1. It adds the owlet for the 2027 hoot format, and is planned for kickoff week (2027-01-16). Until you update, the new hoots are quarantined and doctor says the lake "has Cn hoots, which this Flashpoint can't read" (step 1).
  • The 2027 season file ships, with the 2026 roots and season = 2027. Any WPILib 2027 root changes come in 0.3.1. A configuration made in 2026 reads 2027 from Flashpoint itself, so that fix reaches you when you update, unless you copied seasons/2027.toml into your config folder.
  • doctor stays green on January 1. "Robot for 2027" is a warning while the lake has no 2027 logs. The first 2027 import drafts the robot.
  • Live CAN uses a NetworkTables library held below its 2027 release until 0.3.1 (Live CAN health).
  • Systemcore, the 2027 control system, is untested (#110).

The support matrix has the current status, and #73 tracks the season.

items.title: Set the team name and colours
items.text: The app header can show your team's name and number, and the app can use your team's colours. Both live in theme.toml in your config folder. You can set them when you create the configuration, or later in the Setup view.
path: Set the team name and colours

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• Flashpoint is installed.
  • For the Setup view: flashpoint serve runs on this laptop, started the usual way, and the app is open on this laptop. Shared with --host 0.0.0.0, Setup is read-only.
  • Your colours as #RRGGBB codes, if you want your own instead of a preset, such as #00A3E0.
path: Set the team name and colours

items.title: On a new configuration: flashpoint init
items.text:
init writes theme.toml along with the rest of the config folder. Give it the name and a preset:

flashpoint init --team <number> --team-name "<team name>" --palette blue

The presets are amber (the default), green, blue, red and white, all on a dark background. Leave out --team-name or --palette and init asks for them in a terminal; leave the name blank for none.

init never overwrites a file. If you already have a configuration, it prints a configuration already exists in <folder>; nothing changed: and changes nothing. Use the Setup view instead.
path: Set the team name and colours

items.title: On an existing configuration: the Setup view
items.text:
1. Start the app with flashpoint serve and open SETUP, then CONFIGURATION.
  2. Under APPEARANCE, in TEAM NAME AND COLOURS, fill in:
    • TEAM NAME (HEADER, AT MOST 40 CHARACTERS);
    • TEAM NUMBER (EMPTY: FROM ACQUIRE.TOML), only if the header should show a different number from your team number;
    • COLOURS: a preset, or "custom colours" for your own. Custom colours adds PRIMARY, BACKGROUND (EMPTY: DEFAULT) and WARNING (EMPTY: AUTOMATIC), each as #RRGGBB with a colour picker beside it.
  3. Look at the preview box under the fields. It redraws in the chosen colours, and says whether they're readable.
  4. If it says "Not readable, so it can't be saved:", press the USE PRIMARY or USE WARNING button it offers. That puts the nearest colour that passes in the field.
  5. Press the section's SAVE.
  6. Reload the page. The rest of the app keeps the old colours until you do.

Flashpoint refuses colours that are hard to read: every text shade needs at least 4.5:1 contrast on every background, and the warning colour must stand apart from the primary. The theme.toml reference has the exact rules and every key, if you'd rather edit the file.

A Replay export on a USB stick keeps the name and colours it was written with. Run flashpoint report --static again to update it (Take Replay on a USB stick).
path: Set the team name and colours

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
• After SAVE, the section says "Saved theme.toml. Next: every view, on its next page load (reload the page)."
  • The preview says "✓ Readable: every text shade has at least 4.5:1 contrast on every surface, and the warning colour stands apart from the primary."
  • After a reload, the header reads FLASHPOINT telemetry // and your name and number, such as "Robo Rams · 1234", and the app uses your colours. With no name set, it shows only your team number.

If the app is back to amber with no name, theme.toml doesn't load: flashpoint doctor shows a PROBLEM on theme.toml with the reason. See A settings file doesn't load and the common errors.
path: Set the team name and colours

items.title: Triage an anomaly
items.text:
Status: beta (#77). Detection is tuned on one team's robots (ours), so a finding is a suggestion to check against its evidence, not a verdict.

Triage records what the team did about something detection flagged: someone is looking into it, it was fixed, or it's expected. The note you write is shown the next time the same thing turns up on that motor, so the next student starts from what you found.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• The lake has matches, and detection has run on them. ingest and the automatic import run it for you; to run it by hand, use flashpoint detect. Until it has run, the Anomalies view says "Detection has not run on this lake yet: run flashpoint detect."
  • You're on the laptop running flashpoint serve, started the usual way, and the app is open on that laptop. Triage is saved in the lake, so it only works there. Shared with --host 0.0.0.0, the buttons are replaced by "Read-only: triage is only available on the machine running Flashpoint.", for everyone, the laptop included.
  • You can get to the robot, or ask someone who can: triage is about what you found on it.

items.title: Triage it
items.text:
1. Open the ANOMALIES tab. SHOW is on OPEN: the anomalies that are NEW or INVESTIGATING, highest severity first.
  2. Pick one in the queue. Read its title, ACTUAL and EXPECTED, and WHY IT WAS FLAGGED.
  3. Check the evidence. The EVIDENCE chart shows the metric over the unit's matches, with flagged matches as large dots. Select a point to open that match in Replay, with this slot's tracks, and see what happened.
  4. Read LIKELY CAUSES and SEEN THIS BEFORE: what to check for this kind of finding, and what the team wrote last time.
  5. Press INVESTIGATE when someone starts looking. It saves at once.
  6. When you know the answer, close it:
    • MARK RESOLVED if you found and fixed something. Write what in WHAT WAS FOUND OR FIXED, such as "Loose power lug on the intake Talon, re-crimped".
    • DISMISS AS EXPECTED if it isn't a problem. Write why in WHY THIS IS EXPECTED, such as "New gearbox installed before Q12".
  7. Press SAVE · and the action. The text is required, up to 500 characters.

To bring a closed anomaly back, open it under RESOLVED or DISMISSED and press REOPEN. It goes back to NEW.

items.title: After a deliberate change: restart the baseline
items.text:
DRIFT and STEP compare a unit with its own earlier matches. After you change the mechanism on purpose (a new gearbox, a new ratio), the old normal keeps flagging the new one. When you dismiss such an anomaly, tick "Restart this unit's baseline for metric from the onset match (for example after a gearbox change)". The unit's baseline for that metric then starts again from the match the anomaly started in.

A restart runs flashpoint detect in the background. Until it has run, the anomaly says "Baseline restart pending: detection has not run since the restart was recorded. The queue updates when it does." The unit needs min_baseline matches again (5 by default, anomaly.toml) before DRIFT and STEP judge it.

items.title: Add a cause you found
items.text:
LIKELY CAUSES comes from anomaly-causes.toml. When you resolve an anomaly and the cause wasn't listed, add it so the next student sees it:

  1. Open anomaly-causes.toml in your config folder. flashpoint init puts a copy there; if yours has none, copy the starting list in first.

  2. Add a [[cause]] with the anomaly's method and metric, as the detail shows them, and the subsystem if it applies only there:

    [[cause]]
method = "STEP"
metric = "stator_current_p95"
subsystem = "intake"
text = "Something rubbing or jammed in the intake"

  3. Run flashpoint doctor to check the file loads. The next anomaly you open shows the new cause; no restart is needed.

Every key is in the anomaly-causes.toml reference.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
• After INVESTIGATE, the anomaly's state in the queue and the header reads INVESTIGATING.
  • After SAVE, it moves out of OPEN: SHOW counts it under RESOLVED or DISMISSED. Its detail has an OUTCOME with what you wrote, and HISTORY lists the change with its time ("baseline restarted" when you ticked the box).
  • A refused save shows "Not saved:" and the reason, such as "an outcome is required: say what was found or done".

If doctor shows anomaly-causes.toml doesn't load, or the detail says "The cause catalogue has an error:", see A settings file doesn't load. Every part of the view is in the Anomalies view reference.

items.title: Update Flashpoint
items.text: Update to a new release, and roll back if you need to. Updating replaces the program only: your config folder and your lake are kept, and you don't import anything again.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• Internet on the laptop. Without it, see Install without internet.
  • Read the release notes for the new version: the GitHub Releases page or the changelog. They say when a release needs flashpoint rebuild, or extra steps to go back to an older version.

  • Note the version you have now, in case you want to go back:

    flashpoint --version

  • Stop flashpoint serve (Ctrl-C) and a running flashpoint acquire --watch. A running command keeps using the old version until it's started again.

items.title: Update
items.text:
1. Update with the tool you installed with. With uv, on every computer:

    uv tool upgrade flashpoint

    With pipx on macOS or Linux:

    pipx upgrade flashpoint

    With pipx on Windows:

    py -3.13 -m pipx upgrade flashpoint

  2. Check the setup:

    flashpoint doctor

    If the lake section says <n> file(s) from an older pipeline version: run `flashpoint rebuild`, or the release notes say to, run flashpoint rebuild. It reprocesses those files from the lake's own copies, so you don't need the original logs, then rebuilds Replay data.

    flashpoint rebuild

  3. Start flashpoint serve again, and the watch if you use it. As a service, restart it: systemctl --user restart flashpoint-acquire on Linux, or schtasks /End /TN flashpoint-acquire then schtasks /Run /TN flashpoint-acquire on Windows (Automatic import).

A new season's Phoenix release can change the hoot format. After updating for a new season, ingest one hoot from this season's robot code while you have internet, so Flashpoint downloads the owlet it needs (User guide: Before an event).

If you installed from a checkout, update with git pull, then uv tool install --force --python 3.13 . in the checkout.

items.title: What updating changes
items.text: After an update Config folder Not touched. A settings file you never copied there keeps using the default that ships with the new version Lake Not touched by the update itself. A new version may update the lake's records the first time it opens the lake: 0.2.0, for example, marked files quarantined for a machine error as failed, so they're retried. The release notes say when owlet Kept in ~/.cache/flashpoint/ (or FLASHPOINT_CACHE). A version that reads a new hoot format downloads its owlet on the first such hoot

items.title: Roll back
items.text:
To go back to an older version, install it by number. With uv:

uv tool install --python 3.13 flashpoint==<version>

uv then keeps that version: uv tool upgrade says it's pinned. To return to the newest release:

uv tool install --python 3.13 flashpoint@latest

With pipx:

pipx install --force flashpoint==<version>

Check the release notes of the version you're leaving before you go back. Going from 0.2.0 to an older version, for example, needs a change to the lake first, given in the 0.2.0 notes under "Downgrading".

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
flashpoint --version prints the new version:

$ flashpoint --version
flashpoint <version>

The first line of flashpoint doctor shows the same version and the pipeline version, such as flashpoint 0.2.0 (pipeline v2), and the lake section has no line about files from an older pipeline version.

If flashpoint isn't found after the update, see flashpoint isn't found after installing. If doctor says the lake has C<number> hoots, which this Flashpoint can't read, see Hoots this version can't read.

items.title: Install
items.text: Flashpoint installs with one command on macOS, Linux and Windows. It brings its own Python, so you don't need to install one first.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
A computer running one of: - macOS 13 or later; - Linux with glibc 2.35 or later (Ubuntu 22.04 or later); - Windows on an x86-64 PC (not Windows on ARM).

Flashpoint runs on Python 3.11 to 3.14 (not 3.15 yet). uv installs Flashpoint and, if your computer has no Python in that range, downloads one just for Flashpoint.

You need internet for the install, and once more before your first event to fetch the hoot converter (each OS page says how). To install on a laptop that never goes online, see Install without internet.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Follow the page for your computer: - macOS - Linux - Windows

Each one is the same three steps: install uv once, install Flashpoint, and create your configuration:

uv tool install --python 3.13 flashpoint
flashpoint init --team <your team number>

If you already use pipx, each page also gives the pipx command. pipx needs a Python 3.11 to 3.14 already installed.

items.title: Next
items.text: Import a match and open the app: Quickstart. New to Flashpoint as a team? The team setup tutorial goes through everything in order.

items.title: Install on Linux
items.text: You need Linux with glibc 2.35 or later: Ubuntu 22.04 or later, or another distribution of the same age. ldd --version shows your glibc version. Flashpoint brings its own Python, so you don't need to install one.

items.title: Install
items.text:
1. Install uv, once:

    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

    Open a new terminal afterwards. (uv's installation page lists other ways.)

  2. Install Flashpoint:

    uv tool install --python 3.13 flashpoint

    uv downloads Python 3.13 for Flashpoint if your system doesn't have it. Your system Python isn't touched.

  3. Create your configuration:

    flashpoint init --team <your team number>

    init asks for anything you leave out: your lake folder (where logs and results are stored, ~/flashpoint-lake by default), your team name and the app's colours. It writes your config folder, ~/.config/flashpoint. See flashpoint init.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
flashpoint --version
flashpoint doctor

--version prints flashpoint and a version number. doctor lists the setup checks: right after init, the robot check is a warning until you import this season's logs, which is expected.

If the shell says flashpoint: command not found, run uv tool update-shell and open a new terminal.

items.title: With pipx instead
items.text:
If you already use pipx, it works too, but it needs a Python 3.11 to 3.14 already installed:

pipx install --python python3.13 flashpoint

Use whichever of python3.11 to python3.14 you have.

items.title: Before your first event
items.text:
Flashpoint converts hoot files with CTRE's owlet tool, which it downloads the first time it sees a hoot of each format. Do that while you still have internet: ingest one hoot from this season's robot code, then check that doctor says owlet is downloaded, verified.

flashpoint ingest <a recent .hoot file>
flashpoint doctor

For a laptop that never goes online, see Install without internet.

items.title: Updating
items.text:
uv tool upgrade flashpoint

With pipx, pipx upgrade flashpoint. Your config folder and lake are kept either way. To move from pipx to uv, run pipx uninstall flashpoint, then the uv install above; your config folder and lake aren't touched.

Next: Quickstart.

items.title: Install on macOS
items.text: You need macOS 13 or later. Flashpoint brings its own Python, so you don't need to install one.

items.text:
1. Install uv, once. With Homebrew:

    brew install uv

    Without Homebrew, use uv's installer: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh. Open a new terminal afterwards.

  2. Install Flashpoint:

    uv tool install --python 3.13 flashpoint

    uv downloads Python 3.13 for Flashpoint if your Mac doesn't have it. Nothing else on your Mac changes.

  3. Create your configuration:

    flashpoint init --team <your team number>

    init asks for anything you leave out: your lake folder (where logs and results are stored, ~/flashpoint-lake by default), your team name and the app's colours. It writes your config folder, ~/.config/flashpoint. See flashpoint init.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
flashpoint --version
flashpoint doctor

--version prints flashpoint and a version number. doctor lists the setup checks: right after init, the robot check is a warning until you import this season's logs, which is expected.

If the terminal says flashpoint: command not found, run uv tool update-shell and open a new terminal.

items.title: With pipx instead
items.text:
If you already use pipx, it works too, but it needs a Python 3.11 to 3.14 already installed (Homebrew's newest Python may be too new):

pipx install --python python3.13 flashpoint

Use whichever of python3.11 to python3.14 you have.

Flashpoint converts hoot files with CTRE's owlet tool, which it downloads the first time it sees a hoot of each format. Do that while you still have internet: ingest one hoot from this season's robot code, then check that doctor says owlet is downloaded, verified.

flashpoint ingest <a recent .hoot file>
flashpoint doctor

For a laptop that never goes online, see Install without internet.

items.text:
uv tool upgrade flashpoint

With pipx, pipx upgrade flashpoint. Your config folder and lake are kept either way. To move from pipx to uv, run pipx uninstall flashpoint, then the uv install above; your config folder and lake aren't touched.

Next: Quickstart.

items.title: Install on Windows
items.text: You need Windows on an x86-64 PC; Windows on ARM isn't supported yet. Flashpoint brings its own Python, so you don't need to install one. Run these commands in PowerShell.

items.title: Install
items.text:
1. Install uv, once:

    winget install --id=astral-sh.uv -e

    Without winget, use uv's installer: powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex". Open a new PowerShell window afterwards.

  2. Install Flashpoint:

    uv tool install --python 3.13 flashpoint

    uv downloads Python 3.13 for Flashpoint if your PC doesn't have it. Nothing else changes.

  3. Create your configuration:

    flashpoint init --team <your team number>

    init asks for anything you leave out: your lake folder (where logs and results are stored, %USERPROFILE%\flashpoint-lake by default), your team name and the app's colours. It writes your config folder, %APPDATA%\flashpoint. See flashpoint init.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
flashpoint --version
flashpoint doctor

--version prints flashpoint and a version number. doctor lists the setup checks: right after init, the robot check is a warning until you import this season's logs, which is expected.

If PowerShell says flashpoint isn't recognized, run uv tool update-shell and open a new window.

items.title: With pipx instead
items.text:
pipx needs a Python 3.11 to 3.14 already installed. Windows has no python3.13 command, so use the py launcher: in the python.org installer for Python 3.13, tick "py launcher". Then:

py -3.13 -m pip install --user pipx
py -3.13 -m pipx install flashpoint

items.title: Before your first event
items.text:
Flashpoint converts hoot files with CTRE's owlet tool, which it downloads the first time it sees a hoot of each format. Do that while you still have internet: ingest one hoot from this season's robot code, then check that doctor says owlet is downloaded, verified.

flashpoint ingest <a recent .hoot file>
flashpoint doctor

For a laptop that never goes online, see Install without internet.

items.title: Updating
items.text:
uv tool upgrade flashpoint

With pipx, py -3.13 -m pipx upgrade flashpoint. Your config folder and lake are kept either way. To move from pipx to uv, run py -3.13 -m pipx uninstall flashpoint, then the uv install above; your config folder and lake aren't touched.

Next: Quickstart.

items.title: CLI reference
items.text:
Every Flashpoint command is a subcommand of flashpoint. This page covers what each one is for, every option, and an example. The option tables are generated from the CLI itself (python tools/gen-cli-reference.py), so they match flashpoint <command> --help.

In a source checkout, put poetry run in front of each command (poetry run flashpoint doctor).

items.title: Settings every command shares
items.text:
Setting Default Change it with Lake (where logs and results are stored) lake in acquire.toml, else ~/flashpoint-lake --lake PATH on any command, or FLASHPOINT_LAKE Config folder (team, robots, seasons, thresholds) ~/.config/flashpoint/ (Windows: %APPDATA%\flashpoint) FLASHPOINT_CONFIG Download cache (owlet) ~/.cache/flashpoint/ FLASHPOINT_CACHE

A settings file missing from the config folder falls back to the default that ships with Flashpoint (thresholds, anomaly settings, season roots, the app's colours). doctor lists which files are defaults.

Exit codes: 0 success, 1 failed (for ingest and rebuild: a file failed or was quarantined in this run), 2 usage or configuration error, 3 another Flashpoint process holds the lock, 130 interrupted with Ctrl-C.

items.title: flashpoint init
items.text:
Create your config folder: acquire.toml with your team number and lake folder, theme.toml with the name and colours the app shows, plus copies of the default settings files to edit. Without --team, --lake, --team-name or --palette it asks for them (in a terminal only; leave the name blank for none). It never overwrites a file: run it again and it lists what already exists and changes nothing. The robot addresses acquire tries come from the team number. Of the season files Flashpoint ships, it copies the current season's and earlier ones; a later season is read from Flashpoint itself until you copy it.

It prints each file it created, then the next step: next: import a match's logs with flashpoint ingest <folder> (it drafts your robot from them), then run flashpoint serve.

Option What it does Default --team NUMBER your FRC team number, 1 to 99999 (asked if omitted) --lake LAKE lake folder for your logs (asked if omitted; ~/flashpoint-lake) --team-name NAME name shown in the app header, at most 40 characters (asked if omitted) --palette PRESET app colours: amber, green, blue, red or white (asked if omitted; amber)

With no team name, the header shows your team number from --team ("telemetry // 254"); with neither, it reads just "telemetry". For your own colours instead of a preset, use the Setup view's Appearance section or edit theme.toml.

flashpoint init --team 254 --team-name "The Cheesy Poofs" --palette blue --lake ~/frc-lake

items.title: flashpoint ingest
items.text:
Copy .wpilog and .hoot files into the lake and read them. You can pass files, folders (searched recursively), or both. Files already in the lake are skipped, so re-running is safe. When at least one file was ingested, derive (and so detect) runs afterward on its own, and then the Replay data is rebuilt for the matches that changed (the same build as flashpoint report).

Option What it does Default PATH .wpilog and .hoot files, or folders (searched recursively) --profile {health,all} hoot signals: health (what Flashpoint uses; default) or all (about 3x larger) health --jobs N hoot files converted in parallel (default: half your CPU cores) --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake) --no-derive skip the automatic derive, and so the Replay build too --no-report skip the automatic Replay build after derive --no-robot-draft don't draft a robot file for a season that has none (see Setup > Draft robot) 
flashpoint ingest ~/Downloads/GACMP/

Files that need attention are listed before the summary:

Line Meaning QUARANTINED name: reason The file itself is bad (empty, corrupt, an unknown format). It stays in the lake, unused, and later runs don't try it again FAILED name: failed (reason), will retry The machine failed, not the file: owlet couldn't be downloaded (no internet), crashed, or timed out. The next ingest, rebuild, or acquire cycle tries it again. A file that crashes owlet or times out 3 times is quarantined SKIPPED name: quarantined earlier (reason) The file was quarantined in an earlier run. Retry it with flashpoint rebuild --quarantined WARNING name: ... The file was ingested, but something in it looked off (the warnings are listed)

Then one line counts files ingested, skipped, failed, quarantined, and quarantined earlier. When files were quarantined earlier, a hint to run flashpoint rebuild --quarantined follows it. The exit code is 1 when a file failed or was quarantined in this run. Files quarantined earlier don't change it.

If another Replay build is running (the acquire watch or serve at start), ingest says so; run flashpoint report after it finishes. A failed Replay build prints its error. Neither changes the exit code.

items.title: flashpoint rebuild
items.text:
Reprocess, from its raw copy, every file that an older version of Flashpoint processed, and every file that failed (a machine error such as no internet for the owlet download). restore marks every file this way. Use it when doctor says "N file(s) from an older pipeline version", and after a restore. When it reprocessed anything, derive --all runs afterward, then the Replay build. With nothing to do, it prints 0 ingested and stops. You never need the original logs.

Option What it does Default --profile {health,all} hoot signals: health (what Flashpoint uses; default) or all (about 3x larger) health --quarantined reprocess only quarantined files, from their raw copies, with a fresh 3 tries --no-report skip the automatic Replay build after derive --no-robot-draft don't draft a robot file for a season that has none (see Setup > Draft robot) --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake)

A file whose raw copy is missing is listed as MISSING RAW and left as it is.

flashpoint rebuild
flashpoint rebuild --quarantined

items.title: flashpoint derive
items.text:
Build the match-level data from what ingest read. That means grouping each wpilog with its hoots, aligning their clocks, mapping devices to robot slots and physical units, framing auto and teleop, and computing per-motor match features. Only sessions whose inputs changed are rebuilt. Detection runs at the end.

The first derive drafts your robot. When the lake holds logs from a season that has no robot file in your config folder, derive first drafts one per robot-code project, from the match with the most CAN devices, and saves it as robots/<season>-comp.toml (a second project gets -practice). It prints drafted robot 2026-comp from 2026gacmp_qm7 (22 devices) into ..., and the file's first line says it was drafted. Name each slot's subsystem and role in Setup > Robots, and keep the drafted slot ids. A season that already has any robot file is never touched. Hoot-only logs have no robot-code project, so they draft nothing: use Setup > Draft robot for them. With no configuration (flashpoint init) nothing is drafted, and a read-only config folder is named in a warning. Since ingest, rebuild and the acquire cycle run derive, they draft too.

Option What it does Default --all rebuild every session, not only changed ones (after editing a robot file) --no-robot-draft don't draft a robot file for a season that has none (see Setup > Draft robot) --report then build Replay data for the matches that changed, as ingest does --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake) 
flashpoint derive --all

items.title: flashpoint detect
items.text:
Recompute anomalies. derive already does this, so you only need it after editing anomaly.toml in your config folder (the default); no re-derive is needed. It skips the work when nothing changed.

Option What it does Default --all run even when nothing changed --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake) 
flashpoint detect

items.title: flashpoint backtest
items.text:
Score anomaly detection against the known failures in failure-labels.toml in your config folder (Ignite's is config/failure-labels.toml): which ones were caught, how many matches early, and the false-positive rate. Writes a Markdown report and its data to <lake>/report/backtest/.

Option What it does Default --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake) 
flashpoint backtest

items.title: flashpoint report
items.text:
Build the Replay data for each match, about 1 MB per match. Matches whose inputs haven't changed are skipped. serve runs this for you when it starts, and acquire runs it after each cycle that derives something new, so you only need it on its own for a static export.

Only one build runs on a lake at a time. While another build holds <lake>/meta/report.lock, report exits with code 3 and writes nothing; run it again when that build ends. serve started during a build skips its own build and serves the existing data.

Option What it does Default --event EVENT only this event, e.g. 2026gacmp (repeatable) --match KEY only this match key, e.g. 2026gacmp_qm7 (repeatable) --all rebuild even unchanged matches --static OUT also write a Replay folder that opens from index.html with no server --no-raw with --static: leave the raw logs out (much smaller) --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake) 
flashpoint report --static /Volumes/USB/flashpoint

items.title: flashpoint serve
items.text:
Run the Flashpoint app in your browser: Replay, History, Anomalies, Setup and Live CAN. Builds any missing Replay data first.

Option What it does Default --host HOST bind address (default 127.0.0.1); 0.0.0.0 shares the app, read-only, on the pit network 127.0.0.1 --port PORT port (default 8000; 0 = any free port) 8000 --robot-host ADDRESS robot address for the Live CAN view (repeatable; default: the acquire hosts) --no-build start without building Replay data first --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake)

--host 0.0.0.0 shares the app on the pit network. There's no password, so use it only on a network you trust. Nothing can be changed from the app while it runs this way, not even on this laptop: no triage, no Setup saves or fixes, no Appearance changes, no AdvantageScope launch. The Live CAN view connects to the robot only while it's open (Live CAN health).

flashpoint serve
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/

Stop it with Ctrl-C.

items.title: flashpoint acquire
items.text:
Pull new logs from the roboRIO (over SFTP) and from USB drives plugged into this machine, verify each copy, then ingest and derive them. It never deletes or changes anything on the robot or the drive. On the robot, each file's checksum runs at the lowest CPU priority (nice -n 19) so robot code keeps the processor. Settings come from acquire.toml; see Automatic import.

Pulling from the robot and running acquire as a service (--watch) are beta, tested on one robot; --help says so. Importing from USB drives isn't labelled.

Option What it does Default --watch repeat every poll_s until stopped; this is also how it runs as a service (beta, tested on one robot) --host H [H ...] robot addresses to try instead of the configured ones --include-active also pull logs still being written (tagged incomplete) --dry-run list what would be copied and change nothing (not with --watch) --no-usb don't scan removable drives --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake) 
flashpoint acquire --dry-run
flashpoint acquire --watch

items.title: flashpoint backup
items.text:
Back up the raw logs, the metadata and your configuration files to the rclone remote set as backup.remote in acquire.toml, right now. A running acquire --watch already does this on its own schedule, and this command exits with code 3 while one is running. See Automatic import.

Option What it does Default --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake) 
flashpoint backup

items.title: flashpoint restore
items.text:
Copy a backup into a new, empty lake. Then run rebuild on that lake to regenerate everything else. The backed-up configuration goes into the config folder only if it has no configuration files; otherwise it goes to restored-config/ in the lake, and the config folder is left as it is. See Restore drill.

Option What it does Default --force restore into a lake that already has data (avoid; use a new lake) --remote REMOTE rclone remote:path to restore from (default: backup.remote) --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake)

Restore into a new lake rather than using --force; a restore never overwrites configuration.

flashpoint restore --lake ~/flashpoint-lake-restored
flashpoint rebuild --lake ~/flashpoint-lake-restored

items.title: flashpoint doctor
items.text:
Check the setup. It shows: - the Flashpoint and Python versions; - the config folder, and which settings files are the bundled defaults; - where the lake is, and how many files it holds at each stage; - files that need a rebuild; - the seasons and robots configured; - the last acquire and backup; - which AdvantageScope install was found.

Then it runs the setup checks, one line each, marked ok, WARN, PROBLEM or n/a, with the fix under each warning or problem:

Check A problem when Configuration the config folder doesn't exist (fix: flashpoint init) Each settings file (acquire.toml, report.toml, anomaly.toml, anomaly-causes.toml, theme.toml, seasons, robots, failure-labels.toml) it doesn't load; the message names the file and the bad key Team there's no team number and no hosts in acquire.toml, so acquire can't find the robot Robot for this season no robot file is for the current season Lake the lake folder can't be written (not created yet is only a warning) Backup logs or configuration have waited longer than backup.overdue_h (default 24 hours) for a backup (a failed last attempt is a warning; with no backup configured it reads ok, marked optional). See When a backup is overdue owlet, per hoot format in the lake the matching owlet isn't downloaded, or its checksum doesn't match AdvantageScope the configured path is wrong (not found at all is a warning) Acquire service never a problem: a warning when it isn't installed or running (Linux and Windows), n/a on macOS Python the version isn't 3.11 to 3.14

It changes nothing and downloads nothing. It exits 1 when any check is a problem, else 0. Run it first whenever something looks wrong.

Option What it does Default --lake LAKE lake root (default: $FLASHPOINT_LAKE or ~/flashpoint-lake) 
flashpoint doctor

items.title: acquire.toml
items.text:
acquire.toml holds your team number, the lake folder, and how automatic import reaches the robot and backs up. It lives in your config folder: ~/.config/flashpoint/ on macOS and Linux, %APPDATA%\flashpoint on Windows, or the folder FLASHPOINT_CONFIG names. flashpoint init writes it. Its presence is what makes the folder count as a configuration: without it, ingest and derive warn and map no robot.

Unknown keys are an error, so typos are caught. Every key, with its default:

team = 6829
lake = "/home/pit/flashpoint-lake"
hosts = []
user = "lvuser"
password = ""
