  • No enable-edge alignment yet. Reading AdvantageKit's /DriverStation/Enabled for enable edges would lift alignment to low. It waits for a real AdvantageKit log to check against.
  • Match phases come from the hoots' robot mode, so auto and teleop still frame correctly.

See the support matrix for how well each log setup is supported.

items.title: Battery voltage and the PDH
items.text: Flashpoint doesn't read battery voltage or PDH data yet (#6). Today it uses a battery proxy, and there's nothing to add to robot code for it.

items.title: The battery proxy today
items.text:
Replay's battery track, its brownout markers and brownout findings all use the supply voltage of one device standing in for the battery:

  • the robot file's battery_proxy slot, a low-current device on the main power bus such as the gyro (robot file reference);
  • when there's none, the median SupplyVoltage across the robot's CTRE devices, every 20 ms.

Declare a proxy. A motor makes a bad proxy, and so does the median under heavy load: a stalled motor's own wiring drop reads as a brownout. On Ignite's 2026 robot, the old device-minimum proxy reported six brownouts in one match (6.3–6.7 V) that were intake stalls at about 80 A. A single motor's supply dip shows up instead as its supply path resistance, in History.

items.title: What we plan to read
items.text:
These entry names are planned, not read yet. Logging them now does no harm, and the logs you collect this season will have them when Flashpoint does read them:

Planned entry Type Source /Flashpoint/Power/BatteryVoltage double RobotController.getBatteryVoltage() /Flashpoint/Power/TotalCurrent double the PDH's or PDP's getTotalCurrent()

There's no sample file for these yet, because the names may change before Flashpoint reads them. Follow #6 for the final names.

items.title: Build info
items.text:
Flashpoint reads a string entry named MetaData in the wpilog. Each value is one Key: value line. It uses Project Name to pick the robot file when a season has more than one robot (a practice bot and a competition bot), and also keeps Git Branch and GitDirty. With one robot per season you don't need it; with two and no build info, matches go to robot "unknown".

BuildInfo.java writes it from the gversion Gradle plugin's BuildConstants, which many WPILib teams already use:

  public static void log() {
    StringLogEntry meta = new StringLogEntry(DataLogManager.getLog(), "MetaData");
    meta.append("Project Name: " + BuildConstants.MAVEN_NAME);
    meta.append("Git Branch: " + BuildConstants.GIT_BRANCH);
    meta.append("GitDirty: " + (BuildConstants.DIRTY == 1 ? "Uncommitted changes" : "All changes committed"));
  }

Call BuildInfo.log() once in robotInit(), after DataLogManager.start() (the sample's SignalLoggerSetup.start() does that).

If you don't use gversion yet, the sample project's build.gradle shows the plugin block. MAVEN_NAME is the Gradle project name, which is the project folder's name unless settings.gradle sets rootProject.name.

The project name must equal project in the robot file. Draft robot in the Setup view fills project in from the log.

items.title: CAN bus status
items.text:
CAN bus status gives CAN health each bus's utilisation and error counts, per match phase.

Phoenix 6 reports each bus's health. CanBusStatusLogger.java writes five values per bus, every half second, under /Flashpoint/CANBus/<name>/, where <name> is the bus name your robot code uses (rio, or the CANivore's name such as DriveTrain):

Entry Type Meaning Utilization double Fraction of the bus in use, 0 to 1 BusOffCount integer Times the bus went off (a running count) TxFullCount integer Times the transmit buffer was full (a running count) ReceiveErrorCount integer Receive error counter TransmitErrorCount integer Transmit error counter 
/*
 * A suggestion, not a library: copy it into your robot project and adapt it.
 * Tested with WPILib 2026.2.1, Phoenix 6 26.3.0
 * Docs: https://igniterobotics.github.io/flashpoint/latest/robot-side/bus-status/
 */
package frc.robot.flashpoint;

import com.ctre.phoenix6.CANBus;
import com.ctre.phoenix6.CANBus.CANBusStatus;
import edu.wpi.first.util.datalog.DataLog;
import edu.wpi.first.util.datalog.DoubleLogEntry;
import edu.wpi.first.util.datalog.IntegerLogEntry;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.DataLogManager;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.Notifier;
import java.util.List;

/** Logs CAN bus status to /Flashpoint/CANBus/<name>/ every half second. */
public final class CanBusStatusLogger {
  private record Bus(
      CANBus bus,
      DoubleLogEntry utilization,
      IntegerLogEntry busOff,
      IntegerLogEntry txFull,
      IntegerLogEntry rec,
      IntegerLogEntry tec) {}

  private final List<Bus> buses;
  private final Notifier notifier = new Notifier(this::log);

  /** names: the buses as your robot code names them, e.g. "rio" and "DriveTrain". */
  public CanBusStatusLogger(String... names) {
    DataLog log = DataLogManager.getLog();
    buses = java.util.Arrays.stream(names)
        .map(name -> {
          String prefix = "/Flashpoint/CANBus/" + name + "/";
          return new Bus(
              new CANBus(name),
              new DoubleLogEntry(log, prefix + "Utilization"),
              new IntegerLogEntry(log, prefix + "BusOffCount"),
              new IntegerLogEntry(log, prefix + "TxFullCount"),
              new IntegerLogEntry(log, prefix + "ReceiveErrorCount"),
              new IntegerLogEntry(log, prefix + "TransmitErrorCount"));
        })
        .toList();
    notifier.setName("CanBusStatusLogger");
    notifier.startPeriodic(0.5);
  }

  private void log() {
    for (Bus b : buses) {
      CANBusStatus status = b.bus().getStatus();
      if (!status.Status.isOK()) {
        continue; // skip a failed read rather than logging zeros
      }
      b.utilization().append(status.BusUtilization);
      b.busOff().append(status.BusOffCount);
      b.txFull().append(status.TxFullCount);
      b.rec().append(status.REC);
      b.tec().append(status.TEC);
    }
  }
}

Create it once in robotInit(), for example new CanBusStatusLogger("rio", "DriveTrain");, and keep a reference so the Notifier isn't garbage collected.

Then tell Flashpoint about the bus names in your robot file. In the Setup view, the robot's BUSES table ties each name to its hoot bus (rio, or canivore). Then add five [[signal]] tables per bus (see the robot file reference). Draft robot doesn't add them for you. Each one uses root = "flashpoint", entry = "CANBus/<name>/<Entry>", subsystem = "can", component = "<name>" (the same name as in BUSES), and one metric from utilization, bus_off_count, tx_full_count, receive_error_count and transmit_error_count. CAN health finds them only by those subsystem, component and metric values. Ignite's config/robots/2026-comp.toml has a full set for rio and DriveTrain:

[[signal]]
id = "can-rio-utilization"
root = "flashpoint"
entry = "CANBus/rio/Utilization"
subsystem = "can"
component = "rio"
metric = "utilization"

A bus whose status isn't logged reads "not logged" in CAN health, never zero.

items.title: CAN inventory
items.text:
The CAN inventory gives Flashpoint each CTRE device's factory serial number, so a motor's history follows the physical motor through swaps and rebuilds, not the CAN id it sits on.

The Phoenix diagnostics server runs inside your deployed robot program (port 1250) and lists every CTRE device with its serial number, the same list Tuner X shows. CanInventoryLogger.java asks it once, a few seconds after boot, and writes one JSON string to /Flashpoint/CANInventory:

{"schema": 1, "devices": [
  {"model": "Talon FX", "bus": "rio", "id": 5, "serial": "6E9415C3394C4853"},
  {"model": "Talon FX", "bus": "DriveTrain", "id": 11, "serial": "..."}
]}
  • model, bus, id and serial are required for each device. Extra fields are kept but unused: the sample also logs firmware, which Flashpoint doesn't read yet (#87).
  • If it can't read the list, write {"schema": 1, "error": "<why>"} instead; Flashpoint records the error and uses swap dates for that log.
  • Log it again after a hot swap (for example from a dashboard button), and Flashpoint splits the motor's history at that moment.
/*
 * A suggestion, not a library: copy it into your robot project and adapt it.
 * Tested with WPILib 2026.2.1, Phoenix 6 26.3.0
 * Docs: https://igniterobotics.github.io/flashpoint/latest/robot-side/can-inventory/
 */
package frc.robot.flashpoint;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.node.ArrayNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.node.ObjectNode;
import edu.wpi.first.util.datalog.StringLogEntry;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.DataLogManager;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.Duration;

/** Logs every CTRE device's serial number to /Flashpoint/CANInventory (Flashpoint schema 1). */
public final class CanInventoryLogger {
  private static final URI DEVICES = URI.create("http://localhost:1250/?action=getdevices");
  private static final ObjectMapper JSON = new ObjectMapper();
  private static final StringLogEntry ENTRY =
      new StringLogEntry(DataLogManager.getLog(), "/Flashpoint/CANInventory");

  private CanInventoryLogger() {}

  /** Call once from robotInit(). Runs in the background; never blocks the robot loop. */
  public static void start() {
    Thread thread = new Thread(CanInventoryLogger::run, "CanInventoryLogger");
    thread.setDaemon(true);
    thread.start();
  }

  private static void run() {
    HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build();
    String lastError = "no attempt";
    // Devices take a few seconds to enumerate after boot: retry for about a minute.
    for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 12; attempt++) {
      try {
        Thread.sleep(5000);
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(DEVICES).timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build();
        String body = client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body();
        ArrayNode devices = toInventory(JSON.readTree(body));
        if (devices.size() > 0) {
          ObjectNode inventory = JSON.createObjectNode().put("schema", 1);
          inventory.set("devices", devices);
          ENTRY.append(JSON.writeValueAsString(inventory));
          return;
        }
        lastError = "the diagnostics server listed no devices";
      } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        return;
      } catch (Exception e) {
        lastError = e.toString();
      }
    }
    ENTRY.append(JSON.createObjectNode().put("schema", 1).put("error", lastError).toString());
  }

  /** The diagnostics server's DeviceArray, as Flashpoint's device list. */
  private static ArrayNode toInventory(JsonNode response) {
    ArrayNode out = JSON.createArrayNode();
    for (JsonNode device : response.path("DeviceArray")) {
      String serial = device.path("SerialNo").asText("");
      if (serial.isEmpty()) {
        continue; // not a device that reports a serial
      }
      out.addObject()
          .put("model", device.path("Model").asText())
          .put("bus", device.path("CANbus").asText("rio"))
          .put("id", device.path("ID").asInt())
          .put("serial", serial)
          .put("firmware", device.path("CurrentVers").asText(""));
    }
    return out;
  }
}

Call CanInventoryLogger.start(); at the end of robotInit().

Before you rely on it, open http://<roboRIO address>:1250/?action=getdevices in a browser while the robot program runs. Check that the field names match (DeviceArray, Model, CANbus, ID, SerialNo). The diagnostics server isn't a documented API, and the names can change between Phoenix versions. When the inventory is read, History follows each motor by its serial number (its unit is ctre:<serial>) instead of by slot. Without it, motors get legacy units (how units work).

items.title: The WPILib DataLog
items.text:
The WPILib DataLog (.wpilog) tells Flashpoint which match a log is, when the match phases happened, and the wall-clock time that lines the hoots up with it. Without a wpilog, a session's hoots still import, but its motors get no history: ingest warns

warning: 1 session(s) with hoots but no wpilog (...): their motors get no history (no aligned samples, usage or match features). Motor history needs the robot to write a wpilog too: turn on WPILib data logging (DataLogManager.start()).

items.title: Turn it on
items.text:
SignalLoggerSetup.java does both calls, first thing in robotInit():

    DataLogManager.start();
    DriverStation.startDataLog(DataLogManager.getLog());

Checked 2026-11-21 against WPILib's On-Robot Telemetry Recording page:

  • DataLogManager.start() writes to a logs folder on the USB stick if one is plugged in, and to /home/lvuser/logs otherwise. The stick must be FAT32; NTFS and exFAT don't work.
  • It records every NetworkTables change, and a systemTime entry about every 5 seconds.
  • It doesn't record Driver Station data on its own. DriverStation.startDataLog(DataLogManager.getLog()) adds DS control data (enabled, autonomous, teleop) and joystick data.
  • A file is named FRC_TBD_<random>.wpilog until the Driver Station connects, then FRC_yyyyMMdd_HHmmss.wpilog (UTC), and FRC_yyyyMMdd_HHmmss_<event>_<match>.wpilog once the FMS gives a match.
  • With less than 50 MB free, it deletes the oldest FRC_ logs until there's 50 MB free or 10 files left. At startup it deletes logs from runs where no Driver Station connected. See Disk space.

items.title: What Flashpoint reads from it
items.text:
Entry Used for NT:/FMSInfo/... (NetworkTables, which DataLogManager records) The match: event, match type and number. The file name is the fallback, then The Blue Alliance DS:enabled, DS:autonomous and the other DS entries Match phases (auto, teleop, disabled) and when the robot was enabled systemTime The wall clock, which anchors the log's timestamps MetaData Build info: which robot file the log uses /Flashpoint/... The CAN inventory and CAN bus status NetworkTables entries your robot file maps Whatever signals you map (robot file reference)

Lining hoots up with the wpilog. Flashpoint puts hoot samples on the wpilog's clock. It does that exactly (to well under a millisecond) when one signal is written to both logs, such as DriveState/Pose, which CTRE's swerve code writes to the hoot and to NetworkTables. Otherwise it pairs the robot-enable edges in both logs (DS:enabled and the hoot's RobotEnable), which is good to 30–500 ms, and as a last resort it uses the wall clock.

items.title: Disk space
items.text: A full disk loses logs quietly. Check free space on the roboRIO and its USB stick before each event day, and look for a new hoot after each match (Signal logging).

items.title: What happens when space runs out
items.text:
Checked 2026-11-21 against the WPILib DataLog page and CTRE's signal logging page:

  • wpilogs: with less than 50 MB free, DataLogManager deletes the oldest FRC_ logs until there's 50 MB free or 10 files left. Old matches can disappear before Flashpoint has copied them.
  • Hoots: signal logging stops when less than 5 MB is free, printing Available disk space (3 MB) below 5 MB, stopping log (with the real figure) to the console. WPILib's clean-up doesn't delete hoots, so hoots are usually what fills the disk.

The roboRIO's internal storage is small, so use a USB stick: SignalLoggerSetup.java puts both logs on it when it's plugged in. Format the stick FAT32; the roboRIO doesn't read NTFS or exFAT.

items.title: What Flashpoint does
items.text:
• It never deletes logs on the robot. Clearing space is yours to do, after Flashpoint has copied the files.
  • Robot pull reads the free space of each log folder it copies from. When one is below low_space_mb (100 MB by default, in acquire.toml), the automatic import's log says so (robot <address>: low space on /u/logs: 62 MB free), and flashpoint doctor lists it in its acquire status as low-space <address> /u/logs: <bytes> bytes free. The app doesn't show it, so on an event day run doctor or check the space yourself.

items.title: Clearing space safely
items.text:
1. Import the logs first: from the USB stick or with robot pull.
  2. Check the import worked: each match you're about to delete opens in Replay.
  3. Delete old session folders on the stick (or over SFTP in /home/lvuser/logs), oldest first. Keep the current event's.

items.title: Phoenix Pro and temperature
items.text: Motor temperature is only in a hoot when the log has a Phoenix Pro-licensed device. Without Pro, Flashpoint gets everything else, but no temperature.

items.title: What a free hoot has
items.text:
Checked 2026-11-21 against the "Free Signals" list on CTRE's signal logging page: "Any log that contains a pro-licensed device will export all signals." Without one, only the free list exports. For a Talon FX that's SupplyCurrent, StatorCurrent, MotorVoltage, Position and Velocity (plus SupplyVoltage for every device) and some fault flags, but not DeviceTemp. Only the over-temperature fault flags are free.

So a free hoot has every motor signal Flashpoint uses except temperature. A Pigeon 2 or CANcoder has no temperature Flashpoint tracks at all, Pro or not.

items.title: Why one Pro device is enough for a bus
items.text: CTRE licenses the export per log: "Any log that contains a pro-licensed device will export all signals." Each CAN bus writes its own hoot, so one Pro-licensed device on a bus unlocks that bus's whole hoot, temperature included, for every device on it. A bus with no Pro device gets the free list only. A robot can have both: a Pro CANivore with temperature, and a free rio bus without it. Flashpoint decides per bus.

items.title: What you get without Pro
items.text:
• Works: Replay's current, voltage and velocity tracks, CAN dropouts, stall and brownout detection, History for everything except temperature, and the anomaly findings that don't depend on temperature.
  • Missing: the temperature track and temperature limits in Replay, temperature in History, and thermal findings. Detection never raises a finding because temperature is missing; it skips it, and its summary counts those rows as "not logged (needs Phoenix Pro)".
  • Replay's header names each bus without temperature and says it needs a Phoenix Pro-licensed device. That bus's temperature cells read "not logged (needs Phoenix Pro)".
  • flashpoint doctor and the Setup view's checks report the Phoenix Pro coverage: how many hoots are Pro-licensed, and how many aren't on each bus. It's information, never a warning, because the only fix is buying Pro.

items.title: N/A and NEEDS PRO in History
items.text:
When a unit has no temperature value in range, History's health reads one of three things instead of OK, WARN or HOT:

Health Meaning NEEDS PRO The device reports temperature, but every hoot that carried it was not Pro-licensed. Its latest temperature reads "not logged (needs Phoenix Pro)". N/A Flashpoint tracks no temperature for this kind of device: a CANcoder has no temperature signal, and a Pigeon 2's own temperature isn't tracked. Reads "temperature not tracked", Pro or not. NO DATA The device should report temperature, its hoots were Pro-licensed, and there's still no value: check the log.

All three rank below OK, and none counts toward the "units warn/hot" tile. An open anomaly still raises any of them to WARN or HOT.

Flashpoint reads motor temperature only from hoots. If thermal tracking matters to your team, Pro on the motors you worry about is the way to get it.

items.title: Signal logging (hoots)
items.text: Phoenix 6 signal logging writes every CTRE device's status signals to .hoot files: one per CAN bus. They're Flashpoint's main source of motor data: current, voltage, velocity, temperature (with Phoenix Pro) and the timing that shows CAN dropouts.

items.title: What Phoenix does on its own
items.text:
Checked 2026-11-21 against CTRE's signal logging page:

  • Signal logging is on by default on a roboRIO 2, or a roboRIO 1 with a USB stick. It starts at least 1 second after the robot program starts with the robot enabled, or at least 5 seconds after it starts with the Driver Station connected, whichever comes first. SignalLogger.enableAutoLogging(false) turns that off; then you call SignalLogger.start() and SignalLogger.stop() yourself.
  • Each CAN bus gets its own hoot. A session's hoots go in a subfolder named after the date and time the robot program started.
  • Logging stops when the disk has less than 5 MB free (see Disk space).

CTRE's page doesn't say which folder hoots go to by default, so set it.

items.title: Put the hoots next to the wpilog
items.text:
SignalLoggerSetup.java starts the WPILib DataLog, then points signal logging at the folder the DataLog chose:

  public static void start() {
    DataLogManager.start();
    DriverStation.startDataLog(DataLogManager.getLog());
    if (RobotBase.isReal()) {
      // Hoots land next to the wpilog: on the USB stick when there is one, otherwise
      // /home/lvuser/logs. Flashpoint's robot pull and USB import look in both.
      SignalLogger.setPath(DataLogManager.getLogDir());
    }
  }

So hoots land on the USB stick when one is plugged in, and in /home/lvuser/logs otherwise. Those are the two folders Flashpoint's robot pull reads (roots in acquire.toml), and a USB stick plugged into the laptop is searched four folders deep.

Call SignalLoggerSetup.start() first thing in robotInit(). Keep the default auto-start: it begins before the match does, and the hoots line up with the match through the wpilog's clock.

items.title: Check for a hoot after each match
items.text:
A missing hoot is the most common way to lose a match's motor data, and it's silent on the robot. After each match, in the pit:

  1. Look at the newest session folder on the USB stick (or in /home/lvuser/logs, over SFTP). It should have one .hoot per CAN bus, named like rio_2026-04-12_15-20-31.hoot, with a time just before the match.
  2. Or let Flashpoint check: after an import, open the match in Replay. Its Open in AdvantageScope panel lists the match's logs: one wpilog line, and a hoot · <bus> line for each bus.

If a hoot is missing, check the disk space first, then that the robot code calls SignalLoggerSetup.start() (or that auto-logging wasn't turned off).

items.title: Converting hoots
items.text: Flashpoint converts hoots with CTRE's owlet tool, which it downloads and caches the first time it reads a hoot. That download needs internet, so ingest one hoot at home before you travel. See the support matrix for the hoot versions Flashpoint reads.

items.title: Signal rates
items.text: How often a status signal updates is how often Flashpoint sees it. At 4 Hz a current sample comes every 250 ms, so a 100 ms stall spike can fall between two samples and never show up. Flashpoint wants motor current, voltage, velocity and temperature at 50 Hz (every 20 ms, one sample per robot loop).

items.title: The optimisation caveat
items.text:
Checked 2026-11-21 against CTRE's status signals page: optimizeBusUtilization() disables or slows down every status signal that wasn't given an update frequency. Slowed signals run at 4 Hz by default, which keeps them in the hoot, but only just. So set the rates you need first, then optimise.

This is what happened on Ignite's 2026 robot: the roboRIO-bus Talon FXs logged current, temperature and velocity at 4 Hz, while the CANivore's devices logged at about 250 Hz (#7).

SignalRates.java sets the signals Flashpoint reads to 50 Hz on each motor, then optimises:

  public static void apply(TalonFX... motors) {
    for (TalonFX motor : motors) {
      BaseStatusSignal.setUpdateFrequencyForAll(
          50,
          motor.getStatorCurrent(),
          motor.getSupplyCurrent(),
          motor.getSupplyVoltage(),
          motor.getMotorVoltage(),
          motor.getVelocity(),
          motor.getDeviceTemp());
    }
    ParentDevice.optimizeBusUtilizationForAll(motors);

Call it once in robotInit(), after configuring the motors. Signals that share a status frame update at the highest rate any of them asks for. If you use followers, CTRE's page says the leader must keep DutyCycle, MotorVoltage and TorqueCurrent enabled: add them to the list for leaders.

items.title: The roboRIO bus budget
items.text: The roboRIO's own CAN bus is classic CAN at 1 Mbit/s, and a CANivore's is CAN FD, so the same rates cost the roboRIO bus much more. CTRE warns that above 90 % utilisation the bus behaves unpredictably. With CAN bus status logged, CAN health shows each bus's utilisation per match phase: check the roboRIO bus after raising rates, and if it's high, drop the rate of signals Flashpoint doesn't read (position on motors that don't need it, for example) before dropping current.

items.title: How Replay shows a slow signal
items.text:
When a slot logs current slower than 20 Hz, Replay's header says so, for example:

2 slot(s) log current slower than 20 Hz (indexer, intake); spikes between their samples are not visible.

Stall and brownout times on those slots are rounded to their sample period. Raise their rates, and the note goes away for the next match.

items.title: Your first event
items.text:
A worked example of what you'll do at an event, with real logs: one qualification match from team 6829's robot at the 2026 Georgia district championship. You'll copy the logs off a "USB stick", import them, find the hottest motor, follow it in History, triage what Flashpoint flagged about it, and put Replay on a stick for the drive coach.

It takes about 20 minutes. Everything happens in a folder of its own, with the sample's own configuration, so your configuration and lake aren't touched.

Before you start: - Flashpoint is installed (Install), and you've had internet once, so the hoot converter can download. - You have the sample bundle, flashpoint-sample-1.zip, downloaded and checked: follow the first three lines of Try it with sample logs, in an empty folder.

The commands below are for macOS and Linux, with the Windows (PowerShell) form in the second tab.

items.title: 1. Copy the logs off the stick
items.text:
At an event, the robot writes its logs to a USB stick in the roboRIO. Between matches you pull the stick and copy the new files onto the pit laptop. Here, the bundle's logs/ folder stands in for the stick.

macOS and LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
unzip -q flashpoint-sample-1.zip -d flashpoint-sample
mkdir -p gacmp/q7
cp flashpoint-sample/logs/* gacmp/q7/

Expand-Archive flashpoint-sample-1.zip -DestinationPath flashpoint-sample
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force gacmp\q7
Copy-Item flashpoint-sample\logs\* gacmp\q7\

gacmp/q7/ now has one match's files: the WPILib data log (FRC_20260409_215113_GACMP_Q7.wpilog) and a CTRE hoot for each CAN bus (..._rio_...hoot for the roboRIO's bus, and one named by the CANivore's id). That's what a match looks like on the stick. Import logs from a USB stick has the details for your own robot.

items.title: 2. Import them
items.text:
Point Flashpoint at the sample's configuration (Ignite's robot file, which says which motor is which) and a lake of its own, and import the folder:

macOS and LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
export FLASHPOINT_CONFIG="$PWD/flashpoint-sample/config"
flashpoint ingest --lake "$PWD/gacmp-lake" gacmp/q7

$env:FLASHPOINT_CONFIG = "$PWD\flashpoint-sample\config"
flashpoint ingest --lake "$PWD\gacmp-lake" gacmp\q7

It takes about 10 seconds. The end of what it prints:

derived 1 of 1 session(s)
detected 2 anomalies (0 HIGH, 2 MED, 0 LOW); 22 unit(s) building baseline; scanned through 2026gacmp_qm7
ingested    FRC_20260409_215113_GACMP_Q7.wpilog
ingested    GACMP_Q7_6E9415C3394C485320202050101C18FF_2026-04-09_21-51-06.hoot
ingested    GACMP_Q7_rio_2026-04-09_21-51-06.hoot
3 ingested, 0 skipped, 0 failed, 0 quarantined, 0 quarantined earlier in 10.0s
built 1, unchanged 0, removed 0; 1 match(es) listed in 0.6s

Flashpoint copied the three files into the lake, worked out that they're one match (2026gacmp_qm7), lined the hoots up with the wpilog, ran anomaly detection (two findings) and built the match for Replay. One line before that notes 10 declared signal(s) not written: Ignite's robot file lists CAN bus status entries that this match's robot code didn't log yet. That's expected here.

Run the same command after every match. Files already in the lake are skipped, so you can import the whole stick each time.

items.title: 3. Find the hottest motor in Replay
items.text:
Start the app:

flashpoint serve --lake "$PWD/gacmp-lake"

(PowerShell: flashpoint serve --lake "$PWD\gacmp-lake", in the same window, so FLASHPOINT_CONFIG is still set.) Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/. Replay opens with the match list on the left. Click Q7:

  • The header line says the match lined up with high alignment (payload-match), and shows its robot, start and length.
  • The tracks show the battery (Ignite's gyro is the battery proxy), total supply current, and the hottest motor's temperature, over the whole match. Auto and teleop are shaded.
  • The markers above the tracks are rule hits: Q7 has 12 WARN markers. Click one to jump to it.
  • A note at the top says nine slots log current slower than 20 Hz. On this robot, the roboRIO-bus motors ran at 4 Hz (why that matters).

Now look at the panel on the right. With no cursor on the tracks, it lists match maxima, hottest first:

The top row is intake-extension, the intake's extension leader, at 46 °C. That's well under the 65 °C warning line, so it's healthy, but it's the motor working hardest in this match. Hover over the tracks to see every motor's values at that moment.

items.title: 4. Follow that motor in History
items.text:
Click HISTORY in the header. History shows every motor across every match in the lake. With one match imported there's one point per motor, which is where every motor's history starts. Each match you import adds a point.

In the units table, click intake-extension:

The panel on the right is that motor's record: matches in service, powered-on time, supply energy, thermal cycles, and stall: 21.5 s. A motor stalls when it's pushing hard but barely turning. For an extension that holds against a hard stop, some stall is normal; 21.5 s in one match is a lot. Its unit id is legacy:2026-comp:intake-extension:0: this robot didn't log a CAN inventory yet, so History follows the slot rather than the motor's serial number (CAN inventory).

items.title: 5. Triage what Flashpoint flagged
items.text:
The header's ANOMALIES tab shows 2. Click it. The queue on the left lists both findings, highest severity first. Click Stall time reached 21.5 s in Q7 (expected < 5 s):

It's a MED finding from the SPEC method: a fixed limit (5 s of stall per match) that this motor went past. The evidence chart shows the value per match, and further down, likely causes suggest what to check. Anomalies is beta: treat each finding as a suggestion to look at, not a verdict (Triage an anomaly).

Someone on the team is going to check the extension, so record that. Press INVESTIGATE:

The finding now reads INVESTIGATING, and offers MARK RESOLVED (you fixed something, and say what) and DISMISS AS EXPECTED (it's normal for this mechanism, and say why). Triage is saved in the lake (and its backup), so the next person to open Anomalies sees that it's being looked at. Leave it at INVESTIGATING for now.

items.title: 6. Put Replay on a USB stick
items.text:
The drive coach wants to look at Q7 on their own laptop, which doesn't have Flashpoint. Stop the app with Ctrl-C, then export Replay to a folder (on a real event day, the folder would be on a USB stick):

macOS and LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
flashpoint report --lake "$PWD/gacmp-lake" --static replay-stick --no-raw

flashpoint report --lake "$PWD\gacmp-lake" --static replay-stick --no-raw

It prints exported 1 match(es) to ... with the path of index.html. Open that file in a browser: it's the same Replay, with no server and no internet. --no-raw leaves the log files out, which keeps the folder small; leave it off to include them for download. Take Replay on a USB stick has the rest.

items.title: Check it worked
items.text:
• gacmp-lake/ exists and flashpoint doctor --lake "$PWD/gacmp-lake" runs.
  • Replay listed Q7, and its readout put intake-extension first at 46 °C.
  • Anomalies shows the stall finding as INVESTIGATING.
  • replay-stick/index.html opens Replay in a browser.

To clean up, close this terminal window (so FLASHPOINT_CONFIG goes back to your own configuration) and delete this folder. If a step didn't match what's here, see Troubleshooting.

items.title: Next
items.text:
• Set Flashpoint up for your own team and robot: Setting up Flashpoint for your team.
  • Get more out of your logs: Robot side: what to log. This robot would have had full-rate current on every motor, and serial-number tracking, with the first and sixth rows of that list.

items.title: Setting up Flashpoint for your team
items.text:
This page takes a new FRC team from nothing to a working Flashpoint, in order. Each step is short and links to the page with the details. Flashpoint was built by Ignite Robotics (6829), but nothing in it is tied to Ignite: you give it your team number, your robot and your colours.

What you need: - a pit laptop running macOS, Linux or Windows, with internet for the first setup (what each supports); - robot code that uses CTRE Phoenix 6 motors and writes .wpilog files (most WPILib robots already do); - a few recent logs from your robot (.wpilog and .hoot files), copied off the roboRIO or its USB stick; - about an hour, plus time in the shop to read motor serial numbers with Tuner X.

New to Flashpoint? Try the Quickstart with sample logs first, or the first-event tutorial for a tour of the views.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: 1. What Flashpoint is
items.text:
Flashpoint keeps every log your robot records and tracks the health of each motor over the robot's whole life: temperature, current, stalls, brownouts, and CAN dropouts and reboots. It follows each physical motor by its serial number, so a motor's history goes with it when you move it to another slot or robot, and it flags motors that are drifting away from normal before they cost you a match. You look at the results in a local web app (Replay, History, Anomalies, Setup and Live CAN). Everything runs on one laptop with no internet. Why Flashpoint says more about what it is and isn't.

Flashpoint reads WPILib DataLogs (.wpilog) and CTRE Phoenix 6 signal logs (.hoot). Motor health comes from the hoots, so a robot without Phoenix 6 devices gets much less out of it.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: 2. Install
items.text:
Install with uv, which brings its own Python:

uv tool install --python 3.13 flashpoint

If you don't have uv yet, or flashpoint isn't found afterwards, follow the Install page for macOS, Linux or Windows. For a laptop with no internet at all, see Install without internet.

Two optional extras: rclone, for off-laptop backups (section 7), and AdvantageScope (it comes with WPILib), for Replay's "Open in AdvantageScope" button.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: 3. Create your configuration and import one match
items.text:
Create your configuration, with your own team number and name:

flashpoint init --team 1234 --team-name "Robo Rams" --palette green

In a terminal, init asks for each option you leave out. The example leaves out --lake, so it stops at Lake folder [~/flashpoint-lake]:. Press Enter, or type another folder: the lake holds all your logs and results, so pick a drive with room to grow. init never overwrites anything. It writes your config folder (~/.config/flashpoint/ on macOS and Linux, %APPDATA%\flashpoint on Windows) and prints what it created:

created the configuration in /home/pit/.config/flashpoint:
  acquire.toml
  report.toml
  anomaly.toml
  anomaly-causes.toml
  seasons/2025.toml
  seasons/2026.toml
  units/units-seed.csv
  theme.toml
next: import a match's logs with `flashpoint ingest <folder>` (it drafts your robot from them), then run `flashpoint serve`

Each file has a reference page: acquire.toml (team, lake, robot addresses, backup), theme.toml, report.toml, anomaly.toml, anomaly-causes.toml, seasons and the motor list.

Import one match next, with internet (the first hoot import downloads owlet, the CTRE tool that reads hoots). Copy one match's .wpilog and .hoot files off the robot's USB stick into a folder, then:

flashpoint ingest path/to/one-match/

Since robots/ has no file for that season yet, the import drafts one from the logs and prints drafted robot 2026-comp from 2026gacmp_qm7 (22 devices) into .... You name its slots in section 4. Import logs from a USB stick explains what ingest prints.

Now check the setup:

flashpoint doctor

doctor changes nothing. It prints one line per check, marked ok, WARN, PROBLEM or n/a, with the fix under anything that isn't ok. After this first import, expect a WARN on "Robot for year" while the drafted robot's slots are unnamed, and on AdvantageScope if WPILib isn't installed. Each PROBLEM and its fix is in Troubleshooting.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: 4. Robot side
items.text:
What Flashpoint needs to know about your robot. One robot file per robot per season, in robots/ in your config folder. It lists each CAN device as a slot. Your first import drafted it; to finish it, follow Set up a robot file: name each slot's subsystem and role in Setup > Robots, and keep the drafted slot ids.

What robot code should log. Flashpoint works with the logs your robot already writes, and gets much more from a few additions: the CAN inventory (history follows each motor by serial number), CAN bus status, build info, and status-signal rates high enough to see current spikes. Robot side: what to log ranks them, with Java samples you can copy.

Your motor list. units/units-seed.csv lists every motor the team owns, including spares on the shelf, by serial number, with a label you write on the motor. Fill it in with Tuner X (motor list).
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: 5. Getting logs in
items.text:
By hand: copy logs off the robot or a USB stick into any folder and run flashpoint ingest <folder>. It skips files already in the lake, then works out matches, runs anomaly detection and updates Replay on its own. See Import logs from a USB stick.

Automatically: flashpoint acquire --watch pulls new logs from the robot over the network, and from USB sticks plugged into the laptop. It never deletes or changes anything on the robot or the stick. Robot pull is beta, tested on one robot. See Import logs from the robot automatically, which also sets it up as a service on Linux or Windows.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: 6. Looking at the data
items.text:
flashpoint serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ in a browser, and stop the server with Ctrl-C. Each view has a reference page: Replay, History, Anomalies (beta), Setup and Live CAN (experimental).

To show the app to others, share it on the pit network (no password, read-only) or take Replay on a USB stick. Settings can only be changed from a browser on the laptop running a plain flashpoint serve.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: 7. Backups and moving to another laptop
items.text:
The lake is the only copy of your logs and your anomaly triage, so back it up off the laptop. Flashpoint backs up with rclone to any remote it supports, such as Google Drive, and the watch keeps backing up every 15 minutes. Back up the lake sets it up and walks through the restore drill. Do the drill once before you need it.

When the pit laptop changes, restore from the backup instead of copying folders by hand: Move Flashpoint to another laptop.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: 8. Team name and colours
items.text: The app header shows your team name and number, and the app uses your colours: a preset palette or your own. Set them in Setup > Appearance, which previews them and refuses colours that would be hard to read. See Set the team name and colours, and theme.toml to edit the file by hand.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: 9. Your first week
items.text:
• [ ] Install Flashpoint and run flashpoint init with your team number, name and colours.
  • [ ] With internet, ingest a few recent logs, including at least one .hoot.
  • [ ] Name your robot's slots in Setup, then run flashpoint doctor: "Robot for year" should be ok.
  • [ ] Walk the robot and the spares shelf with Tuner X, label each motor, and fill in units/units-seed.csv.
  • [ ] Add the robot-side loggers (what to log), deploy, and ingest a new log.
  • [ ] Try flashpoint acquire --dry-run with the robot on, then leave flashpoint acquire --watch running.
  • [ ] Set up backup.remote, run flashpoint backup, and do the restore drill once.
  • [ ] Open Replay, History and Anomalies with the students who'll use them at events.
  • [ ] Before your first event, go through the event-day checklist, and ingest one hoot at home so owlet is cached.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: Getting help
items.text:
• Run flashpoint doctor first. Most problems show up there with a fix, and Troubleshooting has the rest.
  • Every command has --help, and the CLI reference covers each one.
  • Ask questions in Q&A discussions, and report bugs with the issue forms. Include the output of flashpoint doctor and flashpoint --version, but never attach match logs to a public issue (share them privately).
  • To change Flashpoint itself, start with the developer guide.
path: Setting up Flashpoint for your team

items.title: Developer guide
items.text: For people who change Flashpoint's code. Read How it works first for the pipeline, the lake, and the identity model. To run Flashpoint without changing it, see the user guide.

items.title: Build and run from source
items.text:
You need: - Python 3.11, 3.12, or 3.13 (requires-python = ">=3.11,<3.14"). pyenv is the easy way to get one; - Poetry 2; - optionally, the GitHub CLI: tools/fetch-corpus.py uses it when it is installed.

git clone https://github.com/IgniteRobotics/flashpoint.git && cd flashpoint
poetry install
poetry run flashpoint doctor

poetry install installs the package in editable mode, along with the dev tools (pytest, ruff, mypy, Playwright, robotpy-wpiutil). The repo's config/ folder is Ignite's team configuration and the tests' fixture. Flashpoint doesn't find it on its own: set export FLASHPOINT_CONFIG=config (from the repo root) in a checkout, or flashpoint uses your per-user folder instead. The tests set it themselves (tests/conftest.py). The shared defaults every team starts from live in src/flashpoint/defaults/ and ship in the package. Optional extras:

poetry install --extras ml        # scikit-learn, for the optional MODEL anomaly detector

Use a scratch lake while developing, so you don't mix test data into your real one:

export FLASHPOINT_LAKE=/tmp/fp-lake
poetry run flashpoint ingest ~/.cache/flashpoint/corpus/corpus-v1/
poetry run flashpoint serve

items.title: Ubuntu notes
items.text:
Ubuntu sets up a few traps for a fresh install:

  • Poetry 1.x from apt. apt install python3-poetry gives you Poetry 1.8. It can't read the [project] table in pyproject.toml, so poetry install fails with "the Poetry configuration is invalid" and complains that name, version, description, and authors are missing. Remove it (sudo apt remove python3-poetry) and install Poetry 2 with pipx: sudo apt install pipx && pipx ensurepath, open a new shell, then pipx install poetry.
  • pyenv shims exit with status 127. That means the selected Python doesn't have the command Poetry ran. If you use pyenv, make a virtualenv and select it in the checkout: pyenv install 3.12, pyenv virtualenv 3.12 flashpoint, pyenv local flashpoint (or pyenv activate flashpoint for one shell). With pyenv global system, the failing command is python: Ubuntu only ships python3. Run poetry env use python3, or sudo apt install python-is-python3.
  • No venv in the system Python. If Poetry builds its venv from Ubuntu's own Python and fails with an ensurepip error, run sudo apt install python3-venv and try again.

items.title: Code layout
items.text:
Path What's there src/flashpoint/cli.py The flashpoint command; one handler per subcommand src/flashpoint/readers/ wpilog reading and hoot conversion (the owlet registry) src/flashpoint/lake/ Lake paths, the ledger, Parquet writing, DuckDB views src/flashpoint/ingest.py ingest and rebuild src/flashpoint/semantics/ derive: sessions, alignment, match identity, framing, device identity, physics, silver, gold, CAN health src/flashpoint/anomaly/ detect and backtest src/flashpoint/report/ Replay data and the static export src/flashpoint/setup/ init, the setup checks behind doctor, the config editor and API, fix actions, and robot drafts: the backend of the Setup view src/flashpoint/theme.py theme.toml: the palette presets, contrast rules, and the colour maths that turns a palette into every colour token src/flashpoint/web/branding.py Builds theme.css and the team name for the page. The server and the static export both use it src/flashpoint/config.py, src/flashpoint/defaults/ Finding and loading configuration; the bundled defaults used when a file is missing src/flashpoint/views/, src/flashpoint/web/ History and Anomalies queries, the HTTP server, the browser app, the AdvantageScope launcher src/flashpoint/acquire/ Robot and USB pulls, the watch loop, backup and restore src/flashpoint/live/ Live CAN: the NetworkTables contract, the detector, the robot connection, and the fake robot (python -m flashpoint.live.fake_robot) src/flashpoint/meta/, src/flashpoint/deploy/ The meta Parquet snapshots; the systemd and Windows service files config/ Ignite's own configuration: acquire.toml, robots, seasons, units, failure labels. A file that isn't here (thresholds in anomaly.toml, report.toml, theme.toml) comes from the bundled defaults in src/flashpoint/defaults/ tools/ fetch-corpus.py, update-owlet-manifest.py, migrate-legacy-config.py examples/robot-java/ The robot-side samples, as a minimal GradleRIO project (./gradlew compileJava with JDK 17; not built in CI) tests/ The test suite, mirroring src/flashpoint/

The code conventions are the coding standards below.

The domain rules (long format at rest, as-of joins with explicit tolerance, never trust filenames over FMS data, offline first, never delete robot logs) are in openspec/config.yaml.

items.title: The browser app
items.text:
• A new view needs three things: a file in src/flashpoint/web/static/views/, an FP.view({ id, label, needsApi, mount, unmount }) call in it, and a <script src="static/views/NAME.js"> tag in web/static/index.html. Without the tag the file never loads. If the view needs the server, add data-needs-api to the tag and set needsApi: true. The static export then leaves the file out and the shell hides the view.
  • Colours come from the role-named tokens in web/static/tokens.css: --accent, --accent-hi, --accent-mid, --accent-dim, --accent-muted, --warn, --on-accent, --prose, the -rgb channel forms (--accent-rgb, --warn-rgb, --bg-rgb), and the colours built from them (--glow-NN, --grid-line). theme.css loads after tokens.css and overrides them with the team's palette; flashpoint.theme derives that map from theme.toml. Never write a colour by hand. tests/web/test_static_lint.py fails on an rgb() or rgba() colour other than black outside tokens.css, on a hex colour in a .css file, and on the old amber names (--amber*, --on-amber, --hot). A hex colour in a .js file is not caught, so check those yourself.
  • Charts can't read CSS variables. Get colours from FP.tokens() (accent, accentHi, accentMid, accentDim, accentMuted, line, lineSoft, lineStrong, warn, accentRgb, surface1, font). They're read once and cached until the page reloads.

items.title: Checks and coding standards
items.text:
poetry run pre-commit run --all-files   # every formatter and linter, at CI's versions
poetry run mypy src tests tools

The first command runs ruff (format and lint), Biome (the app's JS and CSS), and a few file-hygiene hooks, using the versions pinned in .pre-commit-config.yaml. CI runs the same file, so if it passes for you it passes in CI. It fixes what it can and leaves the rest for you. Biome needs Node.js on your PATH; if pre-commit can't set it up, npx @biomejs/biome@2.6.7 check runs the same check. poetry run pre-commit install makes it run on every commit, which is optional.

The JS and CSS were reformatted in one commit when Biome was adopted. Run git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs once so git blame skips it (GitHub's blame view already does).

Coverage is measured on the unit run, with Numba's compiler off so coverage can see the reader kernels:

NUMBA_DISABLE_JIT=1 poetry run pytest --cov

It fails below 93% overall. CI also fails if readers/, lake/, or semantics/physics.py drops below 85%. Floors go up, never down; lowering one needs a mentor's approval in the pull request.

items.title: Coding standards
items.text:
These rules are also the Flashpoint section of the team coding standards. That page is the source: when the two differ, it's right and this section gets fixed. Check rules fail the required CI check. Review rules are a reviewer's job.

Python: formatting, naming, and types

  • Formatting and import order come from ruff format and ruff check. (Check)
  • snake_case functions and variables, PascalCase classes, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants, kebab-case file and folder names outside the Python package. (Check, except filenames: Review)
  • Type hints on everything; mypy --strict passes. (Check)

Why: one style means a diff shows only what changed, and strict types catch a class of bug before the code runs.

Python: suppressions name the rule and the reason

  • # noqa: S608 - table name from the ledger schema, and # type: ignore[arg-type] # fixture dict is untyped. A bare # noqa, a type ignore with no code or no reason, or a suppression for a rule that isn't firing fails the check. (Check)

Why: a suppression claims someone looked at this line. Without a rule it hides every future problem on the line; without a reason nobody can tell if they were right.

Python: processes, shells, and SQL

  • Only the command-line entry point (cli.py, __main__.py) and tools/ exit the process or print. (Check)
  • Subprocesses take an argument list, never a shell string. shell=True, os.system, and os.popen are never allowed, even with a suppression. Each subprocess call says where its arguments come from. (Check)
  • SQL is built only from internal identifiers (lake paths, fixed column and view names); values go in as bound parameters. A line that builds SQL from strings says which identifiers it fills in. (Check)

Why: one bad log calling sys.exit mid-batch stops every log after it (#57). A shell string with a filename in it breaks on a space and can run what the name smuggled in (#54). SQL built from data is the same bug.

Python: errors, time, and complexity

  • No catch-all except except at a boundary that records the error and carries on (a per-file ingest loop, a request handler, a service loop); the suppression names the boundary. A handler that logs the exception passes on its own. (Check)
  • Date-times are timezone-aware. (Check)
  • Functions stay at cyclomatic complexity 12 or under. The nine that were over when this was adopted carry # noqa: C901 - grandfathered (code-quality-gates) and must not get worse. (Check for new code; Review for grandfathered functions)

Why: a catch-all in the wrong place turns a visible crash into silently wrong numbers. Robot logs come from different clocks, and a naive date-time is off by hours without saying so.

Python: tests

  • Every change comes with tests. Unit tests use synthetic fixtures; tests that need real logs are marked corpus. (Review)
  • Coverage stays at or above the floors above. (Check)
  • Once implementation of a change starts, nobody edits its tests to make them pass. (Review)
  • Tests are exempt from a few rules on purpose (asserts, local servers and subprocesses, fixture arguments, compound asserts); see [tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores] in pyproject.toml.

Browser app

  • Classic scripts only: no import/export, no build step. Each file runs in strict mode and touches only the FP namespace, FP_MODE, and uPlot. (Check)
  • Views build the page only through h(). No innerHTML, inline handlers, eval, or new Function (#56). (Check)
  • No remote hosts, and colours only from the role-named tokens (see the browser app). (Check)
  • JS and CSS pass Biome's recommended rules with warnings as errors, and match its formatter. A biome-ignore comment carries a reason. Vendored files are never edited. (Check)

Why: the Replay export opens by double-click from a pit laptop with no network, and browsers refuse ES modules from file://. Log data includes names from robot code, so anything that turns strings into HTML is an injection waiting for the wrong match name.

tests/test_quality.py keeps the gates honest: a deliberately bad file for each check rule (in tests/fixtures/quality/) must fail it, and the suppression and workflow rules are checked there too.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
poetry run pytest                     # unit tests: fast, no data, no network

The default run excludes three markers. Each needs something extra:

Marker Needs Run with corpus The golden log corpus (below) poetry run pytest -m "corpus and not perf and not browser" browser The corpus plus Chromium (poetry run playwright install chromium, once) poetry run pytest -m "browser and not perf" perf The corpus. Checks time and memory budgets poetry run pytest -m perf -s

--strict-markers is on, so a typo in a marker name is an error. Every test has a 300 s timeout. A hang dumps every thread's stack.

The unit suite includes tests/test_docs.py. It fails when a relative link in deploy/README.md or docs/guide/ points at a missing file, when the README has any relative link (the README is also the PyPI page, so every link there must be a full https://github.com/IgniteRobotics/flashpoint/blob/main/... URL to a file that exists), when a flashpoint subcommand has no section in the CLI reference, or when the contract table in Live CAN health doesn't match the code. If you add a subcommand, document it there.

items.title: The golden corpus
items.text:
About 180 MB of real robot logs (release corpus-v1), described with sizes and hashes in tests/corpus/manifest.toml:

poetry run python tools/fetch-corpus.py

It downloads with gh release download if the GitHub CLI is installed (run gh auth login first), otherwise over plain HTTPS, checks every hash, and stores the files in ~/.cache/flashpoint/corpus/corpus-v1/. Set FLASHPOINT_CORPUS_DIR to put them elsewhere, or --from DIR to copy from a local folder. Never replace a corpus file in place; bump the version and publish a new release. Create it with gh release create corpus-vN --latest=false ...: a corpus release must never be the repository's latest release, which belongs to the newest package version. Check with gh release list --json tagName,isLatest: only the newest package version says true.

items.title: Diagrams
items.text:
Diagrams are Mermaid: a fenced code block whose language is mermaid. The docs site draws them with its own copy of Mermaid, and GitHub draws the ones in docs/rewrite/.

A docs diagram must be drawn at 80 % of its natural size or more in the content column of a 1280 px wide window, or its labels shrink below reading size. The pipeline on How Flashpoint works is the example: run left to right, it was 1909 px wide and drew at 36 %, with labels about 5 px high. Run top to bottom, it draws at 100 %. To stay inside the limit: - Run flows top to bottom (flowchart TB). - Put at most about four boxes side by side. - Break long labels yourself with <br>. The docs only wrap a label past 480 px. - Split a diagram that's still too wide into two.

The diagrams in docs/rewrite/ follow the same layout rules when they're next edited.

Boxes are coloured by kind, never in the diagram's source. Tag each box with one of these classes (class A,B data, or A:::data):

Class For Drawn as step A step Flashpoint runs The theme's primary colour data Data Flashpoint keeps Green; draw it as a cylinder, [(name)] robot The robot, or something on it Grey outside Something outside Flashpoint, or optional A dashed outline. Declare classDef outside stroke-dasharray:5 4 in the diagram, so GitHub dashes it too error An error state, in a state diagram Red

The colours come from the docs theme and follow its light/dark toggle. GitHub ignores them and draws the boxes in Mermaid's default colours. A diagram that uses kinds needs a legend right below it, naming each kind it uses and no others:

<div class="fp-legend">
  <span class="fp-legend__item"><span class="fp-swatch fp-swatch--data"></span>data Flashpoint keeps</span>
  <span class="fp-legend__item"><span class="fp-swatch fp-swatch--error"></span>an error state</span>
</div>

Two test files enforce this. tests/test_docs_diagram_scale.py draws every built docs page that holds a diagram and fails on any diagram under 80 %, naming the page, which diagram on it and its size. tests/test_docs_diagram_notation.py checks the classes and legends in each page's source, and, in the browser, the colours in both palettes and that every label is plain text inside its box. The source checks run with the unit tests. The browser checks need Chromium:

poetry run pytest -m browser tests/test_docs_diagram_scale.py tests/test_docs_diagram_notation.py

items.title: CI
items.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml runs on every pull request and on pushes to main and development. A first changes job checks which files changed. When they're all docs (docs/, openspec/, media/, .claude/, and Markdown outside src/ and tests/), only the docs job runs; otherwise everything does.

Job Runs Blocks merge docs Docs-only changes: tests/test_docs.py (links, CLI reference) Through ci-ok lint-test (py3.11) to lint-test (py3.14) Every Python the package declares: pre-commit (ruff, Biome, hygiene hooks), mypy, unit tests, systemd-analyze verify on the service unit. py3.12 adds the ml extra and runs the unit tests with coverage and the floors Through ci-ok windows (py3.12) pre-commit, mypy, unit tests on Windows No, but fix it clean install (<os>, <python>) The built wheel in an empty venv on each OS, with Python 3.11, 3.13 (the documented default) and 3.14: --version, and doctor with no configuration Through ci-ok corpus The corpus tests, including the rclone restore drill Through ci-ok browser (Chromium) The web app in Chromium, served and from file:// Through ci-ok perf (budgets, non-blocking) Time and memory budgets, on pushes to main and development. Allowed to fail; read it when it does No first-run-smoke (separate workflow) A team's first hour on Linux, macOS and Windows, run by tools/first-run-smoke.py: uv tool install --python 3.13 of the wheel, init --team 9999, one corpus match ingested with a real owlet download, Replay must have aligned data, and serve must answer. Nightly, and on PRs that change src/, packaging or the smoke itself; docs-only PRs skip it. Each step names itself when it fails. Run it locally with python tools/first-run-smoke.py (needs uv) No: it gates releases, not merges. A tag's release run calls it on the wheel it built, and PyPI publishing waits for it on all three platforms fresh-install (separate, started by hand) The documented uv tool install --python 3.13 from PyPI (or TestPyPI) with no suitable Python: a clean ubuntu:24.04 container (it also records apt's pipx version), and macOS and Windows runners with uv limited to Pythons it downloads. Then --version and init. Evidence for fresh-machine checks; a hosted runner isn't a fresh laptop No smoke-report (separate, started by hand) The nightly first-run smoke's pass rate per OS over the last N days, with each failure linked (tools/smoke-pass-rate.py); can post it on #71 No codeql (separate workflow) Code scanning for Python and JavaScript, on PRs, pushes, and weekly. A high or critical alert blocks the merge through the ruleset Yes, through the ruleset ci-ok Passes when changes passed, docs or lint-test ran, and none of docs, lint-test, corpus, browser, or clean install failed. The required check Yes

The corpus jobs fetch through gh using the workflow's GH_TOKEN, and cache the corpus and owlet between runs. Every workflow runs with a read-only token unless a job needs more, and actions are pinned to a commit; Dependabot opens one grouped update PR a month for Python packages and one for actions, against development.

items.title: How changes are made
items.text:
Work is planned with OpenSpec, which keeps the plan for each change next to the code:

  • openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md is the current behavior: requirements, each with WHEN/THEN scenarios.
  • openspec/changes/<change>/ holds a change in progress:
  • proposal.md: why;
  • specs/: the requirements it adds or changes;
  • design.md: how;
  • tasks.md: the checklist.
  • openspec/changes/archive/ holds finished changes.

The flow, using the /opsx:* commands in Claude Code (.claude/commands/) or the openspec CLI: 1. Propose (/opsx:propose). Write the proposal, specs, design, and tasks, and validate them with openspec validate <change> --strict. 2. Apply (/opsx:apply). Work through tasks.md, tests first, ticking each task as it's done. 3. Archive (/opsx:archive). Merge the change's specs into openspec/specs/ and move the change to the archive.

Tasks marked [HUMAN] need a person: a pit check, a field test. They stay open until someone does them.

items.title: Branching
items.text:
• development is the integration branch. Each change gets a feature/<name> branch cut from development, and merges back through a pull request with CI.
  • main gets changes only through a pull request from development. Release tags (v*) are cut from main.
  • Both branches are protected the same way: the ci-ok check must pass, a pull request needs one approving review, and only org admins and the code-reviewers team can merge. Nobody can force-push or delete them. Never push to either directly.
  • The rewrite was built on a separate rewrite branch and merged into main on 2026-10-22. The pre-rewrite tree is kept at the legacy-2025 tag.

items.title: Releasing
items.text:
A v* tag on main does the publishing: .github/workflows/release.yml takes the version's section from CHANGELOG.md (and stops, naming the version, if there isn't one), checks the package page for moving or wrong-version documentation links (tools/check-release-links.py), builds, runs the first-run smoke on the built wheel on Linux, macOS and Windows, publishes to PyPI once the smoke has passed everywhere and the pypi environment is approved, and then creates the GitHub Release with that section as its notes. A final version (X.Y.Z) is marked latest; a pre-release (X.Y.Zrc1) is marked as a pre-release and leaves latest alone. A manual run of the workflow publishes to TestPyPI only and creates no GitHub Release.

Follow these steps for every release, in order:

  1. Promote. Move the Unreleased entries in CHANGELOG.md into a ## X.Y.Z - YYYY-MM-DD section, then open a pull request from development to main.
  2. TestPyPI dry run. Run the release workflow by hand from main with an unused X.Y.Z.devN (TestPyPI never takes a version twice, so check which numbers are gone), then install it in a clean venv: pipx install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ --pip-args="--extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/" flashpoint==X.Y.Z.devN.
  3. Smoke on the tag. The cross-platform first-run smoke runs on macOS, Linux and Windows for the commit you're about to tag, and runs again on the tag, where the PyPI publish waits for it. Don't tag over a red smoke.
  4. Clean installs of the dry-run version on macOS, Linux and Windows: flashpoint --version, init, ingest one corpus match, report, and open Replay.
  5. Tag, then approve. git tag vX.Y.Z on main and push it. When the build job passes, approve the pypi environment.
  6. Check the GitHub Release and the latest marker. gh release list shows vX.Y.Z with its changelog section, marked Latest for a final version, and corpus-v* never Latest. If the release job failed after PyPI published, create it by hand: python3 tools/changelog-section.py X.Y.Z > notes.md, then gh release create vX.Y.Z --verify-tag --notes-file notes.md --latest.
  7. Yank policy. Yank a published version only when installing it gives wrong results or breaks. The reason names the version to install instead, for example 0.1.0: "uncapped duckdb/polars; install 0.2.0".
  8. Documentation deploy. Deploy the documentation for the version, so the docs site serves /X.Y/ and latest points at it. A docs-only fix can redeploy the current minor's docs without a package release.

Release-preparation pull requests (the promote PR, changelog moves) reference the release issue as Refs #N and never with a closing keyword. The default branch is development, so a closing keyword there closes the issue as soon as the preparation PR merges, before anything ships. That is how #61 closed early. Close the release issue by hand once the package index shows the version. Feature pull requests keep their closing keyword.

Next patch release: 0.3.1, owner Josh, target 2027-01-16.

items.title: Updating owlet
items.text: CTRE releases new owlet builds for new hoot format versions. The versions and checksums are pinned in src/flashpoint/readers/owlet-manifest.toml. poetry run python tools/update-owlet-manifest.py rewrites that file from CTRE's download index: the newest stable owlet for each format version, on every platform, with checksums computed by downloading each binary. It takes no options besides --help and starts as soon as you run it, so expect several minutes of downloads, and review the diff before committing.

items.title: How Flashpoint works
items.text: This page explains what happens to a log between the robot and the screen. It's written for developers, but nothing here needs code. For the design reasoning and the trade-offs, see the target architecture and the decision records.

items.title: The pipeline
items.text:
flowchart TB
    classDef outside stroke-dasharray:5 4
    R[roboRIO and<br>USB stick] -->|acquire| I[(inbox)]
    M[logs you copied<br>by hand] -->|ingest| RAW
    I -->|ingest| RAW[(raw)]
    RAW --> B[(bronze)]
    B -->|derive| S[(silver)]
    S --> G[(gold)]
    G -->|detect| A[(anomalies)]
    G -->|report| RP[(Replay data)]
    G & A & RP -->|serve| APP[Replay, History, Anomalies,<br>Setup, Live CAN]
    class R robot
    class M outside
    class I,RAW,B,S,G,A,RP data
    class APP step
the robot data Flashpoint keeps a step Flashpoint runs outside Flashpoint Step Command What it does Acquire flashpoint acquire Copies new logs from the robot and USB drives into inbox/, checking each copy by size and SHA-256. See Automatic import Ingest flashpoint ingest Stores each file once in raw/, named by its hash. Converts hoots with CTRE's owlet, and reads every record into bronze/ Derive flashpoint derive (runs after ingest) Groups logs into sessions, aligns clocks, identifies the match and the devices, frames the phases, and writes silver/ and gold/ Detect flashpoint detect (runs after derive) Compares each match against limits, each unit's history, and its siblings, and writes gold/anomalies/ Report flashpoint report (runs after derive, and when serve starts) Builds about 1 MB of Replay data per match in report/ Serve flashpoint serve The web app over all of the above

Each step only redoes work whose inputs changed. Re-running any of them is safe and quick.

ingest and rebuild run derive and then the Replay build, each in its own process. --no-derive (on ingest) and --no-report skip them. The acquire watch cycle does the same.

items.title: What happens to a .hoot file
items.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    direction TB
    [*] --> raw: ingest stores it
    raw --> converted: owlet converts it
    converted --> bronze: every sample read
    raw --> quarantined: the file is bad
    raw --> failed: the machine failed
    failed --> converted: the next run retries
    failed --> quarantined: 3rd crash or timeout
    class raw, converted, bronze data
    class failed, quarantined error
data Flashpoint keeps an error state
  1. Raw: ingest hashes the file. If the ledger has seen that hash, the file is skipped. Otherwise it is copied to raw/<first two hex characters>/<sha256>.hoot (for example raw/3f/3f9a….hoot) and recorded in the ledger (meta/flashpoint.sqlite). Raw files are never changed.
  2. Convert: byte 70 of the file gives its format version. Flashpoint picks the matching owlet build from a versioned registry, downloads it on first use into ~/.cache/flashpoint/owlet/, and converts the hoot. By default it keeps the health signals only (--profile health); --profile all keeps everything. A file that doesn't convert never stops the run. When the file is at fault, it's quarantined with a reason. When the machine is (owlet can't be downloaded, or it crashes or times out), the file is marked failed and the next run retries it. A file that crashes owlet or times out 3 times is quarantined.
  3. Bronze: every sample becomes a row in bronze/samples/ (long format: one row per signal per timestamp). The file's metadata goes to meta/.
  4. Silver: derive puts the hoot in a session with its wpilog, shifts its timestamps onto the wpilog's clock, and maps each Phoenix6/TalonFX-11/... signal to a robot slot and a physical unit. The result goes to silver/samples/.
  5. Gold: derive summarizes each motor for each match phase (energy, current percentiles, temperature, stall time, model residual) into gold/match_features/, one row per match × phase × slot × unit. CAN reboots, dropouts, and bus gaps go to gold/can_health/, gold/can_bus_health/, and gold/can_events/. Each unit's usage in every session, pit and practice included, goes to gold/unit_usage/.

items.title: The lake
items.text:
The lake is one folder (default ~/flashpoint-lake). Everything except raw/ and the ledger is derived from raw/. That's why a backup only needs raw/ and meta/: restore followed by rebuild regenerates the rest.

Folder Holds Rebuildable raw/ The original files, named by SHA-256 No: this is the source of truth inbox/ Files acquire pulled that are waiting to be ingested n/a bronze/samples/ Every decoded sample, partitioned by season and log Yes (from raw; rebuild reprocesses files from older pipeline versions) silver/samples/, silver/signals/ Device samples mapped to slots and units on the wpilog clock; declared NetworkTables signals Yes (derive --all) gold/ match_features, unit_usage, can_health, can_bus_health, can_events, anomalies Yes (derive --all) meta/ The ledger, plus snapshots of logs, sessions, inventory, units, and triage The ledger and triage are not rebuildable; back them up report/ Replay data and backtest reports Yes (report --all)

Data is stored as Parquet and queried with DuckDB (ADR-0001). Transforms use Polars (ADR-0002).

items.title: Sessions and matches
items.text:
A session is everything one robot logged during one power-on: one wpilog plus one hoot per CAN bus (the rio bus and each CANivore).

A session gets a match key like 2026gacmp_qm7, built as season, event, level (pm, qm, or e), and number. The key comes from: 1. the FMS data inside the wpilog; 2. the filename (FRC_yyyyMMdd_HHmmss_EVENT_Q7), only when the log has no FMS match number; 3. nothing. A pit or practice-field session has no key. It still counts toward a unit's usage in History, but it has no Replay entry.

If the filename and the FMS data disagree, FMS wins and the log carries a match-identity-conflict warning.

Framing splits a session into pre-match, autonomous, teleop, and post-match using the robot mode in the hoot (or the Driver Station data in the wpilog), so match features describe the match and not the time in the queue.

items.title: Clock alignment
items.text:
Hoot and wpilog timestamps run on different clocks; the offset was 19.56 s on one real match. Flashpoint aligns each hoot to its wpilog, in this order (ADR-0012):

Method How Confidence payload-match The swerve pose is written to both the hoot and NetworkTables. Identical payloads pair samples exactly High (sub-millisecond) enable-edges Robot-enable edges in both logs, paired one to one and checked against the wall clock Low (30–500 ms) wall-clock The hoot filename time against the wpilog's system time Very low (seconds)

Every match feature carries the weakest alignment confidence in its session.

items.title: Slots and units
items.text:
• A slot is a role on a robot: "front-left drive, CAN ID 11, on the rio bus". Slots are declared in the robot's file in the robots/ folder of your config folder (see the user guide).
  • A unit is a physical motor or device, identified by its CTRE serial number (ctre:<serial>).

The robot code logs a CAN inventory (/Flashpoint/CANInventory) at boot, which tells Flashpoint which unit sits in which slot (ADR-0011). So when a motor moves from one slot or robot to another, its history goes with it.

Logs from before the inventory existed use legacy units (legacy:<robot>:<slot>:<epoch>, such as legacy:2026-comp:drive-bl:0), whose epochs change at swap dates declared in the robot config.

Baselines are per unit. Sibling comparisons are per slot group: the four drive motors, for example.

items.title: Detection
items.text:
detect reads gold only, and every anomaly comes with its evidence and likely causes (ADR-0010).

Kind Fires when SPEC A match breaks a fixed limit, such as temperature or a brownout on the battery proxy DRIFT A unit's metric creeps away from its own baseline over several matches STEP A unit's metric jumps and stays there, e.g. a loosening connector raising supply path resistance SIBLING A unit leaves its sibling group (configured per robot) MODEL Optional. An outlier model, enabled with --extras ml and [model] enabled = true

Brownouts are judged on the battery proxy: the supply voltage of the robot's declared battery_proxy slot (a low-current device on the main power bus, such as the gyro) or, when there is none, the median across devices. A single motor's supply dip is its own wiring drop, not a brownout. That drop instead shows up as supply path resistance (mΩ per motor), a baseline metric, so a loosening connector or lead can surface as a STEP, DRIFT, or SIBLING anomaly.

A unit's baseline is the median of its previous matches, up to 20 by default. A unit with fewer than 5 matches is still "building baseline" and gets no DRIFT or STEP. Severity (HIGH, MED, or LOW) comes from how far outside the baseline the value is. The sensitivity setting in the app (relaxed, normal, or strict) changes what is shown, never what is computed.

Thresholds live in anomaly.toml and likely causes in anomaly-causes.toml in your config folder; the defaults that ship with Flashpoint are anomaly.toml and anomaly-causes.toml. flashpoint backtest scores detection against the known failures in failure-labels.toml (Ignite's is config/failure-labels.toml).

items.title: The app
items.text:
flashpoint serve is one local web app with five views (ADR-0013): - Replay: one match. - History: every unit and slot across matches, events, seasons, and robots. - Anomalies: the anomaly queue, with triage. - Setup: checks your configuration, fixes common problems, and edits the config files, including the team's name and colours. - Live CAN: CAN health read live from the robot over NetworkTables, not from the lake.

The app never changes logs or the lake's derived data. Its only writes are triage rows in the ledger and the config files you edit in Setup.

Replay can also be exported as a static folder that opens with no server. For a single log in depth, Flashpoint hands off to AdvantageScope instead of rebuilding it (ADR-0008, ADR-0014).

The app's colours come from theme.toml in your config folder: a preset palette (amber, green, blue, red, or white) or custom colours. The server turns it into /theme.css, a set of colour tokens loaded after the built-in tokens.css, and shows the team name in the header. If the theme can't be used, the built-in colours apply and the Setup checks say why. A static export copies the theme and team name in force when you export it.

items.title: Querying the lake
items.text:
flashpoint.lake.query.connect opens a DuckDB connection with these views: - samples (bronze); - signals (declared NetworkTables signals); - one meta_<name> view per metadata snapshot, such as meta_logs, meta_sessions, and meta_inventory.

Run these from a checkout with poetry run python:

from flashpoint import config
from flashpoint.lake.paths import LakePaths
from flashpoint.lake.query import connect

con = connect(LakePaths(config.lake_root(None)))
con.sql("select filename, fms_event, fms_match_number from meta_logs").show()
con.sql("""
    select ts_us, v_f64 from samples
    where log_id = (select log_id from meta_logs where filename like 'GACMP_Q7_rio%')
      and signal = 'Phoenix6/TalonFX-1/SupplyCurrent'
""").show()

Gold tables are plain Parquet, partitioned by season and session:

import duckdb

gold = "~/flashpoint-lake/gold/match_features/*/*/*.parquet"
duckdb.sql(f"""
    SELECT match_key, slot_id, round(temp_max_c) AS max_c, round(supply_energy_wh, 2) AS wh
    FROM read_parquet('{gold}', hive_partitioning = true)
    WHERE phase = 'match' AND subsystem = 'drivetrain'
    ORDER BY match_key, slot_id
""").show()

For lifetime questions the app doesn't answer yet, see the marimo notebooks in notebooks/.
